name: सांख्ययोग
teaching: Krishna's first and deepest answer: you grieve over what cannot die, and cling to what cannot stay. Act because action is yours; let go of results because they never were. The chapter ends with a portrait of the person who has actually absorbed this — steady, undisturbed, free. Within one chapter the Gita plants all three of its great seeds — the deathless Self, the right to work without claim on fruits, and the portrait of the steady sage. Everything after is the flowering of these.
questions: What are you currently treating as permanent that is, honestly, passing?
If the results of your work were guaranteed to remain unknown to you, how would you work?
The sthitaprajña withdraws the senses 'as a tortoise draws in its limbs.' What would that look like in one hour of your day?

verses.speaker: सञ्जय उवाच
verses.devanagari:
तं तथा कृपयाविष्टमश्रुपूर्णाकुलेक्षणम् ।
विषीदन्तमिदं वाक्यमुवाच मधुसूदनः॥
verses.transliteration:
taṃ tathā kṛpayāviṣṭamaśrupūrṇākulekṣaṇam
viṣīdantamidaṃ vākyamuvāca madhusūdanaḥ
verses.essence: To him thus overcome by pity, eyes blurred with tears, despairing, Madhusudana speaks.
verses.translation: To him who was thus overcome with pity and who was despondent, with eyes full of tears and agitated, Madhusudana (the destroyer of Madhu) or Krishna spoke these words.

anvaya.base: आ + √विश् · to enter, take hold of
anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, accusative singular (agrees with him)

anvaya.meaning: his eyes full of tears, troubled
anvaya.base: अश्रुपूर्णाकुलेक्षण · whose eyes are tearful and troubled
anvaya.form: compound adjective, masculine, accusative singular (describing him)
anvaya.parts: अश्रु (tears) + पूर्ण (filled) + आकुल (troubled) + ईक्षण (eye): one whose eyes are filled with tears and troubled

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, accusative singular (who is despairing)

anvaya.base: मधुसूदन · slayer of the demon Madhu
anvaya.parts: मधु (the demon Madhu) + सूदन (slayer): the slayer of Madhu

verses.explanation: Sanjaya's camera lingers one moment on the wreckage: pity-possessed, tear-blind, sinking. Then a single shift of name changes everything — the one who now speaks is Madhusūdana, the demon-slayer. Through all of Arjuna's lament Krishna said nothing; he let the despair complete itself. Now that there is nothing left of Arjuna's certainty, the slayer turns to his real target: not Bhishma, not Drona, but the delusion itself.
verses.connection: Picks up Arjuna exactly as 1.47 left him — collapsed — and turns the floor over to Krishna, who has been silent through the whole lament.
verses.reflection: Let someone see your tears today without rushing to explain or end them.
verses.background: Sanjaya narrates the turn: to Arjuna sunk in tears and pity, Krishna breaks his silence — not with consolation but with a bracing rebuke, asking how such unmanliness has come upon him at the very hour of crisis, and commanding him to stand.
verses.hook: In what state is Arjuna when Krishna begins to speak?

views.text: Arjuna's pity is material compassion for bodies, not divine compassion for souls; one so overcome by grief is himself the one in need of mercy.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
कुतस्त्वा कश्मलमिदं विषमे समुपस्थितम् ।
अनार्यजुष्टमस्वर्ग्यमकीर्तिकरमर्जुन॥
verses.transliteration:
kutastvā kaśmalamidaṃ viṣame samupasthitam
anāryajuṣṭamasvargyamakīrtikaramarjuna
verses.essence: Whence comes this stain on you at the crisis hour — ignoble, closing heaven, breeding disgrace?
verses.translation: Whence is this perilous strait come upon thee, this dejection which is unworthy of you, disgraceful, and which will close the gates of heaven upon you, O Arjuna?

anvaya.form: pronoun, accusative singular, short form of त्वाम् (object: you)

anvaya.base: सम् + उप + √स्था · to come near, arise
anvaya.form: past participle, neuter, nominative singular (agrees with this dejection)

anvaya.base: अनार्यजुष्ट · resorted to by ignoble people
anvaya.parts: अनार्य (ignoble person) + जुष्ट (resorted to): that which ignoble people take up
अ (not) + स्वर्ग्य (leading to heaven): that which does not lead to heaven
अकीर्ति (disgrace) + कर (making): that which produces disgrace

verses.explanation: Krishna's first word of reply is a question — kutaḥ, *from where?* — and a hard one. He offers no sympathy, no validation of the eloquent lament; he calls it kaśmalam, a stain, a contamination, and asks where it entered. The diagnosis is brutal because it reframes everything: Arjuna thinks he has seen the truth at last; Krishna treats his vision as a symptom. Three rapid adjectives strip the despair of nobility, of heaven, of honor — every value Arjuna claimed for it. Real teaching often begins by refusing the student's framing of his own problem.
verses.connection: Krishna's answer to the entire first chapter: not a counter-argument, but a question about the source of the arguments.
verses.reflection: When paralysis dresses as virtue, ask the blunt question Krishna asks: where did this come from, now?
verses.background: Sanjaya narrates the turn: to Arjuna sunk in tears and pity, Krishna breaks his silence — not with consolation but with a bracing rebuke, asking how such unmanliness has come upon him at the very hour of crisis, and commanding him to stand.
verses.hook: How does Krishna first respond to Arjuna's despair?

refs.note: Defines an Aryan as a refined, cultured person rather than a race, the ideal Krishna says Arjuna is falling short of.

views.text: The grief is misplaced: it can arise only in people of wrong understanding, blocks the way to heaven, brings no fame, and comes from faint-heartedness.
At first Krishna exhorts by ordinary worldly standards, honour and low birth, and only later imparts knowledge; the rebuke makes Arjuna see that he is taking a fault for a virtue.
Kaśmalam is glossed as moha, delusion, arising in a crisis; it is shunned by noble people and is contrary to dharma as well as to fame.
Instead of comforting him, Krishna makes Arjuna uneasy about his confusion, because that discomfort, rightly channelled, drives a person to seek true knowledge.

verses.devanagari:
क्लैब्यं मा स्म गमः पार्थ नैतत्त्वय्युपपद्यते ।
क्षुद्रं हृदयदौर्बल्यं त्यक्त्वोत्तिष्ठ परन्तप॥
verses.transliteration:
klaibyaṃ mā sma gamaḥ pārtha naitattvayyupapadyate
kṣudraṃ hṛdayadaurbalyaṃ tyaktvottiṣṭha parantapa
verses.essence: Yield not to unmanliness, Partha — it does not become you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and arise, scorcher of foes!
verses.translation: Yield not to impotence, O Arjuna, son of Pritha. It does not befit thee. Cast off this mean weakness of the heart! Stand up, O scorcher of the foes!

anvaya.form: verb, aorist injunctive, 2nd person singular (with मा: a prohibition)

anvaya.parts: हृदय (heart) + दौर्बल्य (weakness): weakness of the heart
पर (enemy) + तप (scorcher): one who scorches enemies

verses.explanation: Two imperatives, no philosophy yet: drop it, stand up. Krishna first tries the warrior's medicine — honor, shame, the names that summon identity: Pārtha, son of the heroic Pritha; Parantapa, scorcher of foes. He calls the grand cascade of chapter 1 kṣudram, *petty* — a small weakness wearing big arguments. It will not work; Arjuna's crisis is too deep for a pep talk, and Krishna surely knows it. But the attempt matters: it establishes that what Arjuna needs is not comfort but a reason to stand, and that no reason of the old kind remains.
verses.connection: Follows the diagnosis of 2.2 with a first prescription — the appeal to honor — which the next verse will show has already failed.
verses.reflection: Find the place where you have called weakness kindness — and stand up inside it, just one inch.
verses.background: Sanjaya narrates the turn: to Arjuna sunk in tears and pity, Krishna breaks his silence — not with consolation but with a bracing rebuke, asking how such unmanliness has come upon him at the very hour of crisis, and commanding him to stand.
verses.hook: What does Krishna tell Arjuna to do with his weakness of heart?

views.text: Both klaibyam and the heart's weakness are glossed as kātarya, timidity, and 'arise' is read specifically as rising for battle.
After rebuking him, Krishna rouses Arjuna's courage, reminding him of his heritage and telling him his feeling is weakness of mind, not true compassion.

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
कथं भीष्ममहं सङ्ख्ये द्रोणं च मधुसूदन ।
इषुभिः प्रतियोत्स्यामि पूजार्हावरिसूदन॥
verses.transliteration:
kathaṃ bhīṣmamahaṃ saṅkhye droṇaṃ ca madhusūdana
iṣubhiḥ pratiyotsyāmi pūjārhāvarisūdana
verses.essence: How shall I fight Bhishma and Drona with arrows, Madhusudana — they who deserve my worship?
verses.translation: How, O Madhusudana, shall I fight in battle with arrows against Bhishma and Drona, who are fit to be worshipped, O destroyer of enemies?

anvaya.base: मधुसूदन · slayer of the demon Madhu
anvaya.parts: मधु (the demon Madhu) + सूदन (slayer)

anvaya.form: compound adjective, masculine, accusative dual (the two)
anvaya.parts: पूजा (worship) + अर्ह (worthy): deserving worship
अरि (enemy) + सूदन (slayer)

verses.explanation: Arjuna answers the call to arms with the two names that make it impossible: Bhishma, Drona. The verse turns on one collision — pūjārhau, 'worthy of worship', against iṣubhiḥ, 'with arrows'. One offers flowers to such men; how does one offer arrowheads? And his choice of address is a quiet counter-thrust: you are Madhusūdana, Arisūdana — slayer of *demons*, of *enemies*. My targets are neither. The objection is real and Krishna never belittles it; he will answer it, but from a depth no one on the field yet suspects.
verses.connection: Direct rebuttal of 'arise' (2.3): standing up means shooting at his grandfather and his guru.
verses.reflection: Name the two 'unattackable' figures in your life — the ones your growth is afraid to confront.
verses.background: Arjuna answers back, still between the armies: how can he shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, worthy of his worship? He would rather beg than rule through their blood — and confesses that no kingdom, not even sovereignty of the gods, could dry the grief withering his senses.
verses.hook: How can Arjuna fight elders he has always revered?

views.text: Arjuna speaks moved by love, compassion and fear, mistaking unrighteousness for righteousness, and not grasping Krishna's beneficial words.
Arjuna insists he holds back not from timidity but because the war is wrong: where even saying 'I will fight them' would be improper, how could he fight them with arrows?
Arjuna asks Krishna not to doubt his courage; his problem is moral, since Bhishma and Drona deserve his reverence, not his arrows.

verses.devanagari:
गुरूनहत्वा हि महानुभावान्
श्रेयो भोक्तुं भैक्ष्यमपीह लोके ।
हत्वार्थकामांस्तु गुरूनिहैव
भुञ्जीय भोगान् रुधिरप्रदिग्धान्॥
verses.transliteration:
gurūnahatvā hi mahānubhāvān śreyo bhoktuṃ bhaikṣyamapīha loke
hatvārthakāmāṃstu gurūnihaiva bhuñjīya bhogān rudhirapradigdhān
verses.essence: Better to live on alms in this world than slay these noble gurus — to kill them is to enjoy pleasures smeared with their blood.
verses.translation: Better it is, indeed, in this world to accept alms than to slay the most noble teachers. But if I kill them, even in this world all my enjoyments of wealth and fulfilled desires will be stained with (their) blood.

anvaya.parts: महा (great) + अनुभाव (dignity, power): those whose dignity is great

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, neuter, nominative singular
compound adjective, masculine, accusative plural (describing the gurus)
anvaya.parts: अर्थ (wealth, gain) + काम (desiring): those who want wealth; some read it instead with भोगान्, 'pleasures of wealth and desire'
रुधिर (blood) + प्रदिग्ध (smeared): smeared with blood

verses.explanation: For a kshatriya, living on bhikṣā — alms — is the deepest humiliation; Arjuna says he prefers it. Yet inside his protest a concession slips out: arthakāmān — these gurus *do* desire wealth, they chose Duryodhana's pay over righteousness, and Arjuna knows it. He honors them and indicts them in the same breath. The closing image is unforgettable: every pleasure won by their death would be rudhira-pradigdhān, blood-smeared. He is saying that some victories contaminate the victor — anticipating, without knowing it, the Gita's teaching that *how* one acts marks the actor more deeply than *what* one wins.
verses.connection: Escalates 2.4: not only can he not fight the gurus — even the fruits of such a fight would be inedible.
verses.reflection: Honor your teachers and still outgrow their conclusions; reverence was never meant to be a ceiling.
verses.background: Arjuna answers back, still between the armies: how can he shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, worthy of his worship? He would rather beg than rule through their blood — and confesses that no kingdom, not even sovereignty of the gods, could dry the grief withering his senses.
verses.hook: Why would Arjuna rather live by begging than kill his teachers?

views.text: The elders are intensely attached to enjoyments; Arjuna asks how he could enjoy the very pleasures they now enjoy once those pleasures are mixed with their blood.
Offers two readings of arthakāmān: pleasures made of wealth and desire, or an epithet of the gurus, greedy for wealth; Bhishma himself later admits he was bound to the Kauravas by wealth.
Arjuna believes a guilty conscience would spoil any wealth or power won by killing his elders, so he would rather beg than commit that crime.

verses.devanagari:
न चैतद्विद्मः कतरन्नो गरीयो
यद्वा जयेम यदि वा नो जयेयुः ।
यानेव हत्वा न जिजीविषामस्-
तेऽवस्थिताः प्रमुखे धार्तराष्ट्राः॥
verses.transliteration:
na caitadvidmaḥ kataranno garīyo yadvā jayema yadi vā no jayeyuḥ
yāneva hatvā na jijīviṣāmaste'vasthitāḥ pramukhe dhārtarāṣṭrāḥ
verses.essence: We do not even know which is better — that we conquer them or they conquer us. Those we would kill stand before us.
verses.translation: I can hardly tell which will be better, that we should conquer them or that they should conquer us. Even the sons of Dhritarashtra, after slaying whom we do not wish to live, stand facing us.

anvaya.form: pronoun, dative plural, short form (for us)
pronoun, accusative plural, short form (object: us)
verb, desiderative present, 1st person plural (wish to)

anvaya.base: धार्तराष्ट्र · son or follower of Dhṛtarāṣṭra

verses.explanation: The warrior's fire of chapter 1 has burned down to honest ash: *we do not know*. Victory and defeat have become indistinguishable, since the victory he is offered requires killing the people who make life worth living. This is the precise shape of a true dilemma — not a hard choice between good and bad, but two paths that both end in loss. Arjuna has reached the most fertile state a student can reach: the end of his own resources. Confessed ignorance is the only soil in which teaching grows.
verses.connection: The certainty of 1.46 ('better to be slain') dissolves into open unknowing — one step from asking for help.
verses.reflection: Sit with one genuine dilemma today without forcing a verdict — let not-knowing be a clean state.
verses.background: Arjuna answers back, still between the armies: how can he shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, worthy of his worship? He would rather beg than rule through their blood — and confesses that no kingdom, not even sovereignty of the gods, could dry the grief withering his senses.
verses.hook: Is it better to win this war or to lose it?

refs.note: Describes Bhishma as a great devotee of Krishna, explaining why his fighting for the Kauravas was not truly against dharma.
Names Bhishma among the twelve great authorities on dharma, underlining the stature of the elder Arjuna cannot bear to fight.

views.text: Arjuna holds that being killed by men who cannot tell right from wrong would be better than winning an unrighteous victory by killing them.
No act proceeds without an intention, and Arjuna cannot form one: no one fights intending defeat, yet here even victory would destroy his own kin.
Even if they accepted the sin of fighting, the outcome is unknown; and since they would not wish to live after killing these men, their victory would in effect be defeat.
Arjuna sees only defeat either way, but his elders sided with the unrighteous; Bhishma, a great devotee, fought for the Kauravas only to serve Krishna's divine purpose.

verses.devanagari:
कार्पण्यदोषोपहतस्वभावः
पृच्छामि त्वां धर्मसम्मूढचेताः ।
यच्छ्रेयः स्यान्निश्चितं ब्रूहि तन्मे
शिष्यस्तेऽहं शाधि मां त्वां प्रपन्नम्॥
verses.transliteration:
kārpaṇyadoṣopahatasvabhāvaḥ pṛcchāmi tvāṃ dharmasammūḍhacetāḥ
yacchreyaḥ syānniścitaṃ brūhi tanme śiṣyaste'haṃ śādhi māṃ tvāṃ prapannam
verses.essence: My nature crippled by pity, my mind confused about dharma, I ask you: tell me decisively what is truly good. I am your disciple — teach me, I have taken refuge in you.
verses.translation: My heart is overpowered by the taint of pity; my mind is confused as to duty. I ask Thee: Tell me decisively what is good for me. I am Thy disciple. Instruct me who has taken refuge in Thee.

anvaya.meaning: my nature struck by faint-hearted pity
anvaya.base: कार्पण्यदोषोपहतस्वभाव · one whose nature is overpowered by weak pity
anvaya.form: compound adjective, masculine, nominative singular (describing I)
anvaya.parts: कार्पण्य (weak pity, faint-heartedness) + दोष (flaw) + उपहत (struck down) + स्वभाव (nature): one whose own nature is struck down by the flaw of faint-heartedness

anvaya.base: धर्मसम्मूढचेतस् · one whose mind is bewildered about dharma
anvaya.form: compound adjective, masculine, nominative singular (describing I)
anvaya.parts: धर्म (duty, right) + सम्मूढ (bewildered) + चेतस् (mind): one whose mind is bewildered about dharma

anvaya.form: pronoun, dative singular, short form (to me)

anvaya.base: शिष्य · pupil, one to be taught

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, accusative singular (describing me)

verses.explanation: The hinge of the entire Gita. Two self-diagnoses — a nature crippled by faint-hearted pity, a mind bewildered about dharma — and then the two sentences that change the relationship forever: śiṣyas te 'ham, I am your disciple; tvāṁ prapannam, I have taken refuge in you. Until this verse Krishna is a charioteer and friend, and teaching cannot be imposed on an equal. By formally becoming a disciple, Arjuna *authorizes* the teaching. And note what he asks for: not consolation, not agreement — śreyas, the real good, niścitam, decisively. The Gita exists because one man, at the bottom of his collapse, asked the right question of the right person.
verses.connection: The unknowing of 2.6 ripens into surrender: the friend becomes a disciple, and the dialogue becomes a scripture.
verses.reflection: Say the rarest sentence aloud to someone wiser: I am confused about my duty — teach me.
verses.background: Arjuna answers back, still between the armies: how can he shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, worthy of his worship? He would rather beg than rule through their blood — and confesses that no kingdom, not even sovereignty of the gods, could dry the grief withering his senses.
verses.hook: What should you do when you no longer know your duty?

refs.note: To know the Absolute, one must approach a guru versed in scripture and established in God; Arjuna now does this with Krishna.
Seekers of the highest good should surrender to a teacher who knows the scriptures and has taken full shelter of God.
Without the guru's grace no one, however elevated, can cross the ocean of material existence.

views.text: This is the moment of surrender: overcome by dejection, Arjuna falls at the Lord's feet and asks, as a disciple who has taken refuge, to be taught what is good for him.

Kārpaṇya is the thought 'how can we live after killing them', the flaw is destroying one's own clan, and the nature struck down is his warrior's valour; he doubts whether begging could be a kṣatriya's dharma.
Here Arjuna, Krishna's friend and cousin, first asks him to be his guru, because divine knowledge for one's lasting good comes through surrender to a genuine spiritual master.

verses.devanagari:
न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्याद्
यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम् ।
अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धं
राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम्॥
verses.transliteration:
na hi prapaśyāmi mamāpanudyād yacchokamucchoṣaṇamindriyāṇām
avāpya bhūmāvasapatnamṛddhaṃ rājyaṃ surāṇāmapi cādhipatyam
verses.essence: I see nothing that could dispel this grief that withers my senses — not unrivalled kingship of the earth, not lordship over the gods.
verses.translation: I do not see that it would remove this sorrow that burns up my senses, even if I should attain prosperous and unrivalled dominion on earth or lordship over the gods.

anvaya.form: adjective (verbal noun), masculine, accusative singular (describing grief)

anvaya.parts: अ (without) + सपत्न (rival): free of rivals

anvaya.form: past participle, neuter, accusative singular (describing kingdom)

verses.explanation: Arjuna shows Krishna the size of the wound so the medicine can be measured. His grief is ucchoṣaṇam indriyāṇām — a drought of the senses, drying him from inside — and he has already run the thought-experiment all the way up: earth's whole kingdom, no; the throne of the gods, no. Nothing *attainable* can cure this. The statement is more important than he knows: by exhausting every possible object, he has proven that the answer cannot be an object. Whatever heals him will have to be a different *kind* of thing — not something to get, but a way to see.
verses.connection: Justifies the surrender of 2.7: he has searched the entire scale of attainment and found no remedy in it.
verses.reflection: Check whether any promotion, success, or escape would actually touch your deepest current ache.
verses.background: Arjuna answers back, still between the armies: how can he shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, worthy of his worship? He would rather beg than rule through their blood — and confesses that no kingdom, not even sovereignty of the gods, could dry the grief withering his senses.
verses.hook: Could even a kingdom over gods and men end Arjuna's grief?

views.text: Read as Arjuna's reply to an unspoken 'then decide for yourself': he can see no course of action that would remove his grief, even if he gained an unrivalled kingdom and the rule of the gods.
Worldly knowledge and gains cannot solve life's deepest sorrows; Arjuna's grief shows that only divine knowledge from a true guru, received with humility, can end it.

verses.speaker: सञ्जय उवाच
verses.devanagari:
एवमुक्त्वा हृषीकेशं गुडाकेशः परन्तप ।
न योत्स्य इति गोविन्दमुक्त्वा तूष्णीं बभूव ह॥
verses.transliteration:
evamuktvā hṛṣīkeśaṃ guḍākeśaḥ parantapa
na yotsya iti govindamuktvā tūṣṇīṃ babhūva ha
verses.essence: Having spoken thus to Hrishikesha, Gudakesha says 'I will not fight,' O King — and falls silent.
verses.translation: Having spoken thus to Hrishikesha (the Lord of the senses), Arjuna (the conqueror of sleep), the destroyer of foes, said to Krishna, "I will not fight" and became silent.

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, accusative singular (person spoken to)
anvaya.parts: हृषीक (senses) + ईश (lord): the lord of the senses
गुडाका (sleep) + ईश (lord, master): master of sleep
पर (enemy) + तप (scorcher)

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, accusative singular (person spoken to)

verses.explanation: Two words and then silence: na yotsye, I will not fight. After the floods of argument, the refusal itself is almost peaceful — and the silence after it (tūṣṇīṁ babhūva) is the most important silence in the poem. It is the silence of a man who has said everything, the empty page on which teaching can finally be written. Sanjaya's irony glints again in the names: Guḍākeśa, conqueror of sleep, declares his surrender to Hṛṣīkeśa, master of the senses. The one in charge of this chariot has just changed.
verses.connection: The discipleship of 2.7 is sealed by renouncing the last word: he states his position and stops talking.
verses.reflection: After declaring 'I will not', notice that you have not left — staying near the question is itself hope.
verses.background: Sanjaya marks the hinge of the whole poem: Arjuna declares 'I will not fight' and falls silent. And Krishna — between the two armies, facing the despondent archer — begins to smile, and speaks the words that open the teaching.
verses.text_note: Variant: parantapaḥ (nominative, describing Arjuna — the reading Sivananda translates) for parantapa (vocative).
verses.hook: What does Arjuna finally tell Krishna before falling silent?

views.text: Here the Lord begins the teaching on the self, judging that Arjuna's delusion would end only through knowing the self's true nature, and that this war, fought without attachment to its fruits, is itself a means to self-knowledge.
Sanjaya's choice of names hints at the outcome: Arjuna, conqueror of sleep, will conquer his despair, and Krishna, master of the senses, will see things set right.

verses.devanagari:
तमुवाच हृषीकेशः प्रहसन्निव भारत ।
सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये विषीदन्तमिदं वचः॥
verses.transliteration:
tamuvāca hṛṣīkeśaḥ prahasanniva bhārata
senayorubhayormadhye viṣīdantamidaṃ vacaḥ
verses.essence: To him despairing between the two armies, Hrishikesha — as if smiling — speaks these words.
verses.translation: To him who was despondent in the midst of the two armies, Krishna, as if smiling, O Bharata, spoke these words.

anvaya.form: pronoun, masculine, accusative singular (person spoken to)

anvaya.parts: हृषीक (senses) + ईश (lord)

anvaya.form: noun, feminine, genitive dual (of the two)
present participle, masculine, accusative singular (describing him)

verses.explanation: One word before the teaching begins: prahasann iva — *as if* smiling. Not laughter at Arjuna's pain; a smile through it, the look of one who can see the whole road from above the fog. The smile says what no argument yet can: from where Krishna stands, this catastrophe is survivable, even luminous. And Sanjaya fixes the location one last time — between the two armies — because that is where every human being receives this teaching: in the middle, committed, unable to retreat into the past or see the way forward. The Gita is taught nowhere else.
verses.connection: Answers the silence of 2.9. Arjuna has emptied himself; Krishna's smile is the first drop of what will fill him.
verses.reflection: Recall a time someone smiled gently at your despair — and how the smile held more truth than pity.
verses.background: Sanjaya marks the hinge of the whole poem: Arjuna declares 'I will not fight' and falls silent. And Krishna — between the two armies, facing the despondent archer — begins to smile, and speaks the words that open the teaching.
verses.hook: How does Krishna look as he begins to answer the grieving Arjuna?

refs.note: Teaches that God sends hardships and calamities so souls do not grow complacent and keep progressing spiritually.

views.text: Everything from 1.2 to 2.9 shows where sorrow and delusion come from, the sources of the round of birth and death; they end only through knowledge of the Self, and that teaching now begins.

Krishna speaks as if in gentle ridicule of a man who grieves from ignorance of body and self yet talks about duty; what follows, up to 18.66, teaches the self, the Supreme Self, and the paths of action, knowledge and devotion.
'Between the two armies' signals that Arjuna had not wholly given up the war: he still asked to be taught, so he is instructed while standing between knowledge and ignorance.
'As if smiling' is glossed as prasanna-mukha: Krishna's face is serene and gracious, not mocking.
Krishna's smile shows the calm of the wise: every situation, pleasant or hard, is arranged by God for our spiritual growth, so the knowing are not shaken by it.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
अशोच्यानन्वशोचस्त्वं प्रज्ञावादांश्च भाषसे ।
गतासूनगतासूंश्च नानुशोचन्ति पण्डिताः॥
verses.transliteration:
aśocyānanvaśocastvaṃ prajñāvādāṃśca bhāṣase
gatāsūnagatāsūṃśca nānuśocanti paṇḍitāḥ
verses.essence: You grieve for those who need no grief, yet speak words of wisdom. The wise mourn neither the living nor the dead.
verses.translation: Thou hast grieved for those that should not be grieved for, yet thou speakest words of wisdom. The wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead.

anvaya.meaning: those not to be grieved for
anvaya.base: शोच्य (from √शुच् · to grieve) · to be mourned
anvaya.form: gerundive with negative अ-, masculine, accusative plural (object)
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + शोच्य (to be grieved for): those who should not be mourned
प्रज्ञा (wisdom) + वाद (speech, argument): words of the wise

anvaya.base: गतासु · one whose life has gone
anvaya.parts: गत (gone) + असु (life-breath): those whose life-breath has departed

anvaya.base: अगतासु · one whose life has not gone
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + गत (gone) + असु (life-breath): those whose life-breath has not departed

verses.explanation: The teaching proper begins, and its first sentence carries a sting: you talk like a paṇḍit and grieve like a man who has understood nothing. Your sorrow is sincere, your words sound wise, and the two have nothing to do with each other. Arjuna's arguments — dharma, family, sin — had the vocabulary of wisdom, but wisdom is not measured by vocabulary; it is measured by what one mourns. The truly wise grieve neither for the dead nor for the living, because they no longer mistake what a person *is*. With this verse the Gita quietly relocates the entire battlefield: the problem is not Bhishma's body across the field, but Arjuna's idea of what Bhishma is. Everything until 2.30 unfolds from this single correction.
verses.connection: The first sentence of the promised teaching (2.10): it answers none of Arjuna's arguments and instead dissolves their shared premise.
verses.reflection: Audit your griefs today: which mourn what is truly lost, and which mourn what cannot be lost?
verses.background: Krishna's first instruction begins. With the armies frozen around the chariot, he addresses the root of Arjuna's grief rather than its occasion: the deathless, unborn, all-pervading Self that weapons cannot cut — the wisdom called Sankhya, delivered to a warrior who believed he was about to commit murder.
verses.hook: Is grief for the living or the dead ever truly justified?

views.text: Paṇḍitas are knowers of the Self (paṇḍā is wisdom about the Self); like a madman, Arjuna displays folly and learning together, grieving for those who are eternal in their real nature.

Arjuna's 'words of wisdom' are his talk of ancestors losing their offerings (1.42), which assumes a self distinct from the body; yet he grieves, so he knows neither the self nor duty as a means to it.
Two reasons in one word: the body is not to be mourned because it is perishing every moment, and the soul is not to be mourned because it never perishes.
Grief comes from failing to tell body from self; 'the living' here are the survivors, whom the wise do not pity by asking how they will live without their kin.
Krishna cuts through Arjuna's reasoning: the wise never lament, and like Bhishma, those surrendered to God do their duty and accept every outcome as grace.

verses.devanagari:
न त्वेवाहं जातु नासं न त्वं नेमे जनाधिपाः ।
न चैव न भविष्यामः सर्वे वयमतः परम्॥
verses.transliteration:
na tvevāhaṃ jātu nāsaṃ na tvaṃ neme janādhipāḥ
na caiva na bhaviṣyāmaḥ sarve vayamataḥ param
verses.essence: Never was there a time when I was not, nor you, nor these kings — and never shall any of us cease to be.
verses.translation: Nor at any time indeed was I not, nor thou, nor these rulers of men, nor verily shall we ever cease to be hereafter.

anvaya.parts: जन (people) + अधिप (ruler): ruler of people

verses.explanation: Krishna's first metaphysical claim, delivered as a triple negative made of granite: there is no past in which we were not, no future in which we will not be. *I, you, these kings* — he sweeps the entire battlefield, both armies, into a single deathless company. If existence has no edges, then the sword that seems to end a person only ends an appearance. Arjuna's whole lament assumed that death subtracts someone from reality; Krishna begins by denying that reality can be subtracted from.
verses.connection: Grounds 2.11: the reason the wise do not mourn is that no one, ever, actually stops existing.
verses.reflection: Look at someone and silently note: this one existed before this body and continues beyond it.
verses.background: Krishna's first instruction begins. With the armies frozen around the chariot, he addresses the root of Arjuna's grief rather than its occasion: the deathless, unborn, all-pervading Self that weapons cannot cut — the wisdom called Sankhya, delivered to a warrior who believed he was about to commit murder.
verses.hook: Did we exist before this life, and will we exist after it?

refs.note: States that God, the soul and Maya are all eternal, so the soul's existence does not end with the body.

views.text: All of us are eternal as the Self in past, present and future; the plural 'we' follows the many bodies, not any real multiplicity of the Self.

By saying I, you, these and we, the Lord himself declares that the difference between God and individual selves, and among the selves, is real and eternal, which rules out the view that difference is only appearance.
The 'I' is the Lord, who exists even as his playful forms appear and vanish; the kings too have always existed, being his portions, and so are not to be grieved for.
Divine knowledge begins with knowing the self: the self is the soul, not the body, and it is eternal like God, which implies life continues after the body dies.

verses.devanagari:
देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा ।
तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति॥
verses.transliteration:
dehino'sminyathā dehe kaumāraṃ yauvanaṃ jarā
tathā dehāntaraprāptirdhīrastatra na muhyati
verses.essence: As the embodied one passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it passes to another body. The steady are not deluded by this.
verses.translation: Just as in this body the embodied (soul) passes into childhood, youth and old age, so also does it pass into another body; the firm man does not grieve thereat.

anvaya.base: देहिन् · one who has a body, the self

anvaya.parts: देह (body) + अन्तर (other) + प्राप्ति (attaining): the attaining of another body

anvaya.form: adjective as noun, masculine, nominative singular (subject)

verses.explanation: The first analogy, drawn from what everyone has already survived. The body of your childhood is gone — every proportion changed — yet *you* did not die when it went. You have already crossed several bodies within this one life and called it growing. Krishna extends the line one segment further: dehāntara-prāpti, reaching another body, is one more such crossing, no more a terminus than your tenth birthday was. The argument is from experience, not scripture. The dhīra — the steady one — is simply someone who follows this continuity without flinching at the largest gap.
verses.connection: Makes 2.12 walkable: eternal existence demonstrated from the ordinary experience of outliving one's own childhood.
verses.reflection: You have already survived several selves — childhood, youth. Trust the continuity that survived them.
verses.background: Krishna's first instruction begins. With the armies frozen around the chariot, he addresses the root of Arjuna's grief rather than its occasion: the deathless, unborn, all-pervading Self that weapons cannot cut — the wisdom called Sankhya, delivered to a warrior who believed he was about to commit murder.
verses.hook: If the body keeps changing, what in you stays the same?

views.text: When boyhood ends the Self is not destroyed, and when youth comes it is not born; the unchanging Self takes on each state, and taking on another body is exactly the same.
Eternal selves take bodies suited to their beginningless karma; to escape that bondage they do their prescribed duties, like war, without attachment, enduring the pleasure and pain of sense contact.
If a change of form called for grief, one would mourn the passing from boyhood to youth; wisdom comes easily to one who is not attached even to this present body, so seek it.

The recognition 'I am the same' across life's stages shows the self survives change; the move to a new body happens through the subtle body, as a newborn's instinct to suckle shows impressions from before.
Just as we pass through many changing bodies in one lifetime yet remain the same person, at death the soul simply moves into another body.

verses.devanagari:
मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौन्तेय शीतोष्णसुखदुःखदाः ।
आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास्तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत॥
verses.transliteration:
mātrāsparśāstu kaunteya śītoṣṇasukhaduḥkhadāḥ
āgamāpāyino'nityāstāṃstitikṣasva bhārata
verses.essence: Contacts of the senses, Kaunteya, give cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go, impermanent — endure them, Bharata.
verses.translation: The contacts of the senses with the objects, O son of Kunti, which cause heat and cold, pleasure and pain, have a beginning and an end; they are impermanent; endure them bravely, O Arjuna.

anvaya.meaning: contacts of the senses with objects
anvaya.parts: मात्रा (sense faculty, that which measures objects) + स्पर्श (contact): the contacts of the senses with their objects

anvaya.base: शीतोष्णसुखदुःखद · producing cold, heat, pleasure and pain
anvaya.parts: शीत (cold) + उष्ण (heat) + सुख (pleasure) + दुःख (pain) + द (giving): that which gives cold and heat, pleasure and pain

anvaya.base: आगमापायिन् · that which arrives and departs
anvaya.parts: आगम (coming) + अपायिन् (going away): that which comes and goes
अ (not) + नित्य (lasting)

anvaya.form: imperative, 2nd person singular, middle voice (a command)

verses.explanation: From the deathless self, Krishna turns briefly to what *does* fluctuate: sensation and feeling. Cold and heat, pleasure and pain — these are mātrā-sparśāḥ, contacts of the senses with their objects, weather passing through awareness. Their signature is āgamāpāyinaḥ: they arrive, they leave; arrival guarantees departure. The instruction is one word: titikṣasva — bear them, let them pass without building a self out of them. This is not suppression but outlasting. Arjuna's anguish, too, is weather. That is not a dismissal of his pain but its correct classification: real, intense, and *transient*.
verses.connection: Pre-empts the objection to 2.13: 'but the grief is unbearable.' Grief belongs to the class of things that pass.
verses.reflection: Next discomfort that arrives, whisper: this is weather, it comes and goes — and watch it obey.
verses.background: Krishna's first instruction begins. With the armies frozen around the chariot, he addresses the root of Arjuna's grief rather than its occasion: the deathless, unborn, all-pervading Self that weapons cannot cut — the wisdom called Sankhya, delivered to a warrior who believed he was about to commit murder.
verses.hook: How should you deal with pleasure and pain that come and go?

views.text: Mātrā are the senses, by which sounds and the like are measured; cold and heat are named apart from pleasure and pain because they please at one time and pain at another, while pleasure and pain are fixed.
These contacts are to be endured with courage until one's prescribed duties are done; when the karma that binds is destroyed, the coming and going itself ends.
The contacts are with the sense organs, not directly with the Supreme Self; their 'coming' is birth and their 'going' destruction.
Mātrā are the workings of the senses; just as water and sun give cold and heat, so meeting and parting with loved ones give joy and sorrow, and bearing them befits a steady person.
Sense pleasures and pains are passing like seasons; a discerning person learns to tolerate both rather than swing between them like a pendulum.

verses.devanagari:
यं हि न व्यथयन्त्येते पुरुषं पुरुषर्षभ ।
समदुःखसुखं धीरं सोऽमृतत्वाय कल्पते॥
verses.transliteration:
yaṃ hi na vyathayantyete puruṣaṃ puruṣarṣabha
samaduḥkhasukhaṃ dhīraṃ so'mṛtatvāya kalpate
verses.essence: The person whom these do not torment, steady in pain and pleasure alike — that one is fit for immortality.
verses.translation: That firm man whom, surely, these afflict not, O chief among men, to whom pleasure and pain are the same, is fit for attaining immortality.

anvaya.form: verb, causative present, 3rd person plural (cause pain)

anvaya.parts: पुरुष (man) + ऋषभ (bull, the foremost): foremost among men

anvaya.base: समदुःखसुख · equal in pain and pleasure
anvaya.form: compound adjective, masculine, accusative singular (describing the person)
anvaya.parts: सम (equal) + दुःख (pain) + सुख (pleasure): one to whom pain and pleasure are equal

verses.explanation: Endurance is given its prize. The one whom sensations cannot vyathayanti — shake, pierce — has discovered something in himself that the weather does not touch; and only what the changing cannot touch can be amṛta, deathless. The logic is exact: equanimity is not stoic decoration, it is the *evidence* of immortality, the immortal part showing through. Sama-duḥkha-sukha — equal in pain and pleasure — appears here for the first time and will become one of the Gita's signature measurements of a free human being.
verses.connection: Completes 2.14: why endure? Because the capacity to stand unshaken is itself the doorway to the deathless of 2.12–13.
verses.reflection: Practice being the same person in praise and in pain for one whole hour today.
verses.background: Krishna's first instruction begins. With the armies frozen around the chariot, he addresses the root of Arjuna's grief rather than its occasion: the deathless, unborn, all-pervading Self that weapons cannot cut — the wisdom called Sankhya, delivered to a warrior who believed he was about to commit murder.
verses.hook: What kind of person is ready for immortality?

views.text: The wise man stays free of joy and sorrow under pleasure and pain because he has realized the eternal Self; enduring the opposites, he becomes fit for immortality, meaning Liberation.
Immortality comes to one who treats pain as as inevitable as pleasure and fights without attachment, untroubled even by the blows of weapons, not to one who, like Arjuna now, cannot bear grief.
Things are not un-lamentable merely because they pass: birth cannot give being to what has none, and what has gained being can never become non-existent.
Titikṣā, calm endurance, is one of the six virtues of a seeker; it strengthens the will, but leads to liberation only when joined to discrimination and dispassion.
As tiny parts of God, an ocean of bliss, we seek infinite, lasting happiness, which sense pleasures can never give; seeing this, we learn to rise above pleasure and pain.

verses.devanagari:
नासतो विद्यते भावो नाभावो विद्यते सतः ।
उभयोरपि दृष्टोऽन्तस्त्वनयोस्तत्त्वदर्शिभिः॥
verses.transliteration:
nāsato vidyate bhāvo nābhāvo vidyate sataḥ
ubhayorapi dṛṣṭo'ntastvanayostattvadarśibhiḥ
verses.essence: The unreal never comes to be; the real never ceases to be. Seers of truth have seen the boundary of both.
verses.translation: The unreal hath no being; there is non-being of the real; the truth about both has been seen by the knowers of the Truth (or the seers of the Essence).

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + सत् (being, real): that which is not real

anvaya.form: verb, present, 3rd person singular (passive form: is found)
verb, present, 3rd person singular (passive form: is found)
present participle of √अस् as noun, genitive singular (of)

anvaya.parts: तत्त्व (truth, reality) + दर्शिन् (seer): those who see things as they are

verses.explanation: The chapter's philosophical summit, two laws in one sixteen-syllable line: what is unreal (asat) never gains being; what is real (sat) never loses it. Everything Arjuna fears losing — bodies, relations, kingdoms — belongs to the order that was always arriving and departing; it never possessed permanent being to lose. What truly *is* cannot be threatened, by arrows or by anything. Grief, examined to its root, is a confusion of these two columns — mourning the asat as if it were sat. The commentators fill the columns differently: Shankara puts every changing thing on the asat side, as a pot is nothing apart from its clay; Ramanuja reads asat as the perishable body and sat as the imperishable self. The tattva-darśins are simply those who have stopped filing things in the wrong column.
verses.connection: Generalizes 2.14–15 into ontology: the passing and the permanent are two different orders of reality, and they never trade places.
verses.reflection: Of all that distresses you now, ask which part will exist in ten years — give attention accordingly.
verses.background: Krishna's first instruction begins. With the armies frozen around the chariot, he addresses the root of Arjuna's grief rather than its occasion: the deathless, unborn, all-pervading Self that weapons cannot cut — the wisdom called Sankhya, delivered to a warrior who believed he was about to commit murder.
verses.hook: What is truly real, and what is only passing?

refs.note: Speaks of three entities, the enjoyer, the enjoyed and the controller, which together make up all that exists.
The Lord supports the perishable and the imperishable, the manifest and the unmanifest, showing God, soul and Maya are eternal.
God created the world and then entered it, pervading everything; so the world cannot be unreal, only temporary.

views.text: Every experience holds two awarenesses: one that changes (pot, cloth) and one that does not ('is'); what the awareness of 'is' never leaves is real, while changing things, nothing apart from their causes, are unreal.
Asat is the body, whose nature is to perish, and sat is the self, whose nature is not to perish; the verse is about discriminating these two, not about the theory that effects pre-exist in causes.
Cold, heat and the rest have no existence in the self, since they are not its properties, and the self never ceases; with this discrimination Arjuna can endure them.
God, soul and Maya are eternal, while bodies and objects are temporary; the world is passing, not non-existent, since God pervades it and even realized saints still use it.

verses.devanagari:
अविनाशि तु तद्विद्धि येन सर्वमिदं ततम् ।
विनाशमव्ययस्यास्य न कश्चित्कर्तुमर्हति॥
verses.transliteration:
avināśi tu tadviddhi yena sarvamidaṃ tatam
vināśamavyayasyāsya na kaścitkartumarhati
verses.essence: Know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded. None can destroy the imperishable.
verses.translation: Know that to be indestructible, by Which all this is pervaded. None can cause the destruction of That, the Imperishable.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + विनाशिन् (perishing)
अ (not) + व्यय (decay, loss)

anvaya.form: indefinite pronoun, masculine, nominative singular (with न: no one)

verses.explanation: What is the sat of the previous verse? Krishna gives its first positive description: it is *that by which all this is pervaded* — tatam, woven through, as space pervades every room without being any room's furniture. Pervading all, it has no outside from which an attack could come; weapons are *within* what they would have to destroy. The argument is quietly devastating to Arjuna's fear: you cannot make a hole in that which is the fabric.
verses.connection: Names the 'real' of 2.16 by its property: all-pervading, and therefore beyond the reach of any destroyer.
verses.reflection: Feel the one aliveness running through every person you meet today; you cannot injure that.
verses.background: Krishna's first instruction begins. With the armies frozen around the chariot, he addresses the root of Arjuna's grief rather than its occasion: the deathless, unborn, all-pervading Self that weapons cannot cut — the wisdom called Sankhya, delivered to a warrior who believed he was about to commit murder.
verses.hook: What is it in you that can never be destroyed?

refs.note: Locates the soul in the heart, from where its consciousness spreads through the body.
Also says the soul dwells in the heart, supporting the soul's local seat in the body.
Like sandal paste on the forehead cooling the whole body, the soul in the heart spreads consciousness everywhere.

views.text: 'That' is Brahman, pervading the universe as space pervades pots; having no parts and nothing of its own to lose, it cannot decay, and no one, not even God, can destroy his own Self.
The individual self pervades all insentient matter and is subtler than anything; since destroying agents like weapons, water and fire must penetrate what they destroy, nothing can destroy the self.
The self pervades the body and all that comes and goes as its witness; that pervasion as witness is what makes it free from destruction.
The soul pervades the body by spreading its consciousness through it, the way a flower's fragrance fills a garden, though the soul itself sits in the heart.

verses.devanagari:
अन्तवन्त इमे देहा नित्यस्योक्ताः शरीरिणः ।
अनाशिनोऽप्रमेयस्य तस्माद्युध्यस्व भारत॥
verses.transliteration:
antavanta ime dehā nityasyoktāḥ śarīriṇaḥ
anāśino'prameyasya tasmādyudhyasva bhārata
verses.essence: These bodies of the eternal embodied one — indestructible, immeasurable — are said to have an end. Therefore fight, Bharata.
verses.translation: These bodies of the embodied Self, Which is eternal, indestructible and immeasurable, are said to have an end. Therefore fight, O Arjuna.

anvaya.base: शरीरिन् · one who has a body, the self

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + नाशिन् (perishing)

anvaya.base: अप्रमेय · not measurable, not an object of knowledge
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + प्रमेय (measurable, knowable)

anvaya.form: pronoun, ablative singular used as indeclinable (from that: therefore)
imperative, 2nd person singular, middle voice (a command)

verses.explanation: The two columns are now placed side by side: bodies — antavantaḥ, end-having, with expiry written into them; the embodied one — eternal, indestructible, immeasurable. And then the sentence that shocks every first reader: *therefore fight*. The 'therefore' does not mean killing is trivial; it means Arjuna's specific reason for refusing — that he would be *destroying* Bhishma and Drona — rests on a metaphysical error. He cannot destroy them; no one can. What the war decides is the fate of bodies and kingdoms, things already mortgaged to time. This is the teaching's first touch of the actual battlefield, and it lands deliberately early: the full ethics of *why* fight — duty, and action without attachment — is still to come.
verses.connection: Draws the practical edge of 2.16–17 for the first time: from the indestructibility of the self, the command to act returns.
verses.reflection: Care for the body as a borrowed instrument — fully, lovingly, without confusing it for the musician.
verses.background: Krishna's first instruction begins. verses.hook: If the body must perish, what about the one living within it?

views.text: 'Eternal' and 'indestructible' are not repetitive: they exclude both kinds of destruction, vanishing and being transformed; 'immeasurable' means the Self is not known by perception, being self-evident to every knower.

Bodies are composite and exist to experience karma, so they perish; the self is never an object but always the knowing subject, partless and pervading, and so imperishable; therefore fight without attachment to fruits.
Bodies are not destroyed only at the end: they change at every moment, and their final disappearance is merely when that constant change becomes visible.
Aprameya means unlimited; since the self neither perishes nor is touched by pleasure and pain, give up grief born of delusion and fight: do not abandon your own dharma.
The body is made from earth and returns to earth, but the soul within it is not made of matter; that eternal soul is the real self.

verses.devanagari:
य एनं वेत्ति हन्तारं यश्चैनं मन्यते हतम् ।
उभौ तौ न विजानीतो नायं हन्ति न हन्यते॥
verses.transliteration: ya enaṃ vetti hantāraṃ yaścainaṃ manyate hatam ubhau tau na vijānīto nāyaṃ hanti na hanyate
verses.essence: Who thinks it a slayer, and who thinks it slain — both fail to understand. It slays not, nor is it slain.
verses.translation: He who takes the Self to be the slayer and he who thinks It is slain, neither of them knows. It slays not, nor is It slain.
verses.explanation: A verse so exact it doubles as a koan (the Katha Upanishad says it almost verbatim, and Emerson rewrote it as 'If the red slayer think he slays...'). Two errors are struck down with one stroke: the victim's error — *I can be killed* — and the killer's error — *I kill*. Both arise from identifying the self with the body's transactions. Note carefully what this does and does not say: it does not absolve the *person* who pulls the trigger of responsibility — karma and dharma govern that, and the Gita will hold Arjuna fully to them. It says the *Self* was never party to the transaction at all.
verses.connection: Closes the loophole left by 2.18: not only can the self not be slain — it is not the slayer either. Agency, like mortality, belongs to another layer.
verses.reflection: Drop both stories today: I can destroy, and I can be destroyed. Act from what remains.
verses.background: Krishna's first instruction begins. With the armies frozen around the chariot, he addresses the root of Arjuna's grief rather than its occasion: the deathless, unborn, all-pervading Self that weapons cannot cut — the wisdom called Sankhya, delivered to a warrior who believed he was about to commit murder.
verses.hook: Can the true self ever kill or be killed?

refs.note: Pain from a dream of being beheaded lasts until we wake; likewise fear of death lasts while we identify with the body.
The Vedic injunction not to harm any living being, which underlies Arjuna's sense that killing his kin would be sinful.

views.text: Being changeless, the Self is neither the agent nor the object of killing; Arjuna's thought 'I am the killer of Bhishma and the others' is simply false.
'Killing' means separating a body from its self, never destroying the self; so scriptural bans on killing still apply, forbidding unsanctioned separation of body and self.
Having removed grief over the deaths of Bhishma and others, Krishna now removes Arjuna's second sorrow, that he would be their killer, voiced in 'I do not wish to kill them'.
Fear of death comes from identifying with the body; yet harming a body is still violence, and when violence is justified, as for Arjuna, Krishna will explain later.

verses.devanagari:
न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन्
नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः ।
अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो
न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे॥
verses.transliteration:
na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ
ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṃ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre
verses.essence: It is never born and never dies; having been, it never ceases to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient — it is not slain when the body is slain.
verses.translation: It is not born, nor does It ever die; after having been, It again ceases not to be; unborn, eternal, changeless and ancient, It is not killed when the body is killed.

anvaya.form: present passive participle, neuter locative singular (when … is being)
noun, neuter locative singular (in/when — with the participle: 'when the body is slain')

verses.explanation: The chapter's great bell-verse, tolling four names of the deathless: aja, unborn; nitya, eternal; śāśvata, everlasting; purāṇa, ancient-yet-ever-fresh. Birth and death are events — and events need a timeline; the self *is* the witness in which timelines appear, so no event can happen *to* it. The verse is the Katha Upanishad speaking inside the Gita, nearly word for word — the teaching's pedigree displayed. And its last line gives Arjuna the sentence he most needs, plain enough to carry into battle: na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre — it is not slain when the body is slain. Two different things are happening on a battlefield; only one of them can be done with arrows. The body is slain; the dweller is not.
verses.connection: Gives the reason behind 2.19: the self neither slays nor is slain because it undergoes no change at all — no birth, no death, no decay — and supplies the formula that directly answers the dread of 1.28–31.
verses.reflection: Sit quietly and find the part of you that has never aged a single day.

verses.hook: Is the self ever born, and does it ever die?

refs.note: An almost identical verse: the soul is unborn, eternal, ageless, and not destroyed when the body is destroyed.
Calls the soul great, unborn, deathless, free from old age, immortal and fearless.

views.text: Reads the verse as denying all six changes of a living thing — birth, existence, growth, change, decay, death — one word at a time; 'na hanyate' is taken as 'is not transformed', so the line does not merely repeat 'does not die'.

Notes the present tense: the birth and death everyone sees in every body never touch the self. 'Having been, it will not cease' refers to the cycle of world-ages: the many individual selves outlast each dissolution.
Maps each word to one denied change: nitya rules out growth, śāśvata rules out decline, and purāṇa means 'new even long ago', so it never becomes new by turning into something else.
The soul is free from the six changes of the body, from conception to death; what we call death touches only the body, never the self.

verses.devanagari:
वेदाविनाशिनं नित्यं य एनमजमव्ययम् ।
कथं स पुरुषः पार्थ कं घातयति हन्ति कम्॥
verses.transliteration:
vedāvināśinaṃ nityaṃ ya enamajamavyayam
kathaṃ sa puruṣaḥ pārtha kaṃ ghātayati hanti kam
verses.essence: Knowing it indestructible, eternal, unborn, immutable — whom does such a person slay, Partha, whom cause to be slain?
verses.translation: Whosoever knows It to be indestructible, eternal, unborn and inexhaustible, how can that man slay, O Arjuna, or cause to be slain?

anvaya.form: verb, perfect form with present sense, 3rd person singular
adjective, masculine accusative singular (describing the object)

verses.explanation: The knowledge is now turned into a question aimed straight at Arjuna's conscience: for one who *knows* this, where exactly is the victim? The verse covers both hands — hanti, slays directly; ghātayati, causes to slay — touching Arjuna's double fear of striking and of commanding strikes. The question is rhetorical at the level of the self, but it is preparing something further: if the deepest 'I' neither kills nor is killed, then action can perhaps be performed without the knot of *doership* — the thread Krishna will pick up when he turns from metaphysics to karma-yoga at 2.39.
verses.connection: Turns the doctrine of 2.20 into a pointed question: for one who knows this, whom is he killing — and so what does Arjuna think he would be doing to Bhishma?
verses.reflection: Knowing the indestructible in others, ask: whom could you still treat as disposable?

verses.hook: If the self cannot be destroyed, who is really killing whom?

views.text: The question is an emphatic denial. Killing is only the example: the knower, being one with the changeless Self, is denied every kind of action, not just slaying or causing others to slay.
The thought 'I am slaying these selves, I am having them slain' rests entirely on ignorance of what the self is, whether it lives in a god, an animal or a plant.
The causative 'ghātayati' is aimed at Krishna himself: the verse also tells Arjuna not to blame Krishna for being the one who urges him to fight.
One who drops the ego of doership sees that the soul does nothing and is untouched by action; Krishna urges Arjuna to act from that state and not shirk his duty.

verses.devanagari:
वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय
नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि ।
तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णा-
न्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही॥
verses.transliteration:
vāsāṃsi jīrṇāni yathā vihāya navāni gṛhṇāti naro'parāṇi
tathā śarīrāṇi vihāya jīrṇānyanyāni saṃyāti navāni dehī
verses.essence: As a man casts off worn-out garments and takes new ones, so the embodied one casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.
verses.translation: Just as a man casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so also the embodied Self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others which are new.

anvaya.base: जीर्ण · worn out, old (√जॄ · to wear out)
देहिन् · one who has a body (the self)

verses.explanation: The Gita's most beloved analogy, chosen for its precise emotional work. Clothes matter — they are fitted, worn daily, even loved — but no one stands at a wardrobe grieving a threadbare coat, because the wearer was never the garment. The image performs a complete reversal of perspective: death, seen from the body's side, is destruction; seen from the self's side, it is *changing*. For Arjuna staring at the aged Bhishma, his body long since 'worn out', the analogy is almost tender: what the arrows would take from the grandfather is the coat. Vāsāṃsi jīrṇāni — 'worn-out garments' — is perhaps the most quoted image of death in Indian literature, and its point is not doctrine first but de-dramatization.
verses.connection: Gives 2.20–21 its unforgettable picture; abstraction becomes wardrobe, and dread loosens into familiarity.
verses.reflection: Think of death once today as a change of clothes — and notice what loosens in your chest.

verses.hook: What happens to the self when the body wears out?

refs.note: A baby's unexplained joy, sorrow and fear are taken as memories of a past life, evidence for rebirth.
A newborn's instinct to suckle is explained by practice in countless past lives.

views.text: The embodied one, the Self, stays unchanging like the man in the example: only the bodies wear out and are replaced, as clothes are, while the wearer remains the same.
Scripture teaches that those who fall in a righteous war gain finer bodies than before; trading worn clothes for beautiful new ones is a cause for joy, not grief.
The stress is on survival: a well-dressed man whose garment wears out simply dresses again and does not perish with the cloth; so the self, clothed in one body after another.
Answers the objection 'the self survives, but I grieve the body': bodies are produced by karma and their end is inevitable, so the loss of a worn-out body leaves no room for grief.
Like changing worn-out clothes, the soul leaves an old body and takes a new one while remaining itself; rebirth also explains why people are born so unequal.

verses.devanagari:
नैनं छिन्दन्ति शस्त्राणि नैनं दहति पावकः ।
न चैनं क्लेदयन्त्यापो न शोषयति मारुतः॥
verses.transliteration:
nainaṃ chindanti śastrāṇi nainaṃ dahati pāvakaḥ
na cainaṃ kledayantyāpo na śoṣayati mārutaḥ
verses.essence: Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, waters do not wet it, wind does not wither it.
verses.translation: Weapons cut It not, fire burns It not, water wets It not, wind dries It not.
verses.explanation: Krishna inventories every destroyer the ancient world knew — blade, flame, flood, gale: the four elements as four weapons — and reports each one's failure. The rhythm itself is the argument: na... na... na... na..., a fourfold door shutting. Why can nothing touch it? Because cutting, burning, wetting, drying are all *transactions between forms*, and the self is not a form among forms — it is the awareness in which forms appear. On a field bristling with literal weapons, Arjuna is told: every one of them is aimed at clothing.
verses.connection: Tests the 'wearer' of 2.22 against all four elemental destroyers — extending 'cannot be slain' to 'cannot be so much as scratched.'
verses.reflection: Name the deepest thing in you, and verify: no insult burned it, no loss drowned it.
verses.background: Krishna's first instruction begins. With the armies frozen around the chariot, he addresses the root of Arjuna's grief rather than its occasion: the deathless, unborn, all-pervading Self that weapons cannot cut — the wisdom called Sankhya, delivered to a warrior who believed he was about to commit murder.
verses.hook: Can anything in the material world harm the self?

views.text: The reason is partlessness: a sword cuts off limbs, water breaks down what is made of parts by soaking it, wind destroys by drying out moisture — none of which can happen to what has no parts.
Cutting, burning, wetting and drying all work by entering a substance. The self is subtler than every element and pervades them, so they cannot pervade it and cannot act on it.
Because the soul is divine and beyond matter, no material force, whether weapon, fire, water or wind, can touch it.

verses.devanagari:
अच्छेद्योऽयमदाह्योऽयमक्लेद्योऽशोष्य एव च ।
नित्यः सर्वगतः स्थाणुरचलोऽयं सनातनः॥
verses.transliteration:
acchedyo'yamadāhyo'yamakledyo'śoṣya eva ca
nityaḥ sarvagataḥ sthāṇuracalo'yaṃ sanātanaḥ
verses.essence: Uncuttable, unburnable, unwettable, undryable — it is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, everlasting.
verses.translation: This Self cannot be cut, burnt, wetted, nor dried up. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable and ancient.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + क्लेद्य (to be wetted): 'not able to be wetted'

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + शोष्य (to be dried): 'not able to be dried'
सर्व (all, everywhere) + गत (gone): 'present everywhere'

verses.explanation: The four failures of 2.23 are recast as four impossibilities — not 'weapons do not cut it' but acchedya, *uncuttable*: invulnerability is its nature, not its luck. Then five positive names in a single exhale: eternal, all-pervading, stable, unmoving, everlasting. The verse works like liturgy; its sound is meant to settle into the body the way its meaning settles into the mind. Tradition treats these repetitions kindly: what the intellect accepts in one hearing, the heart accepts only after many. Krishna is not informing Arjuna anymore — he is *soaking* him.
verses.connection: Seals 2.23 by upgrading resistance into impossibility, and lets repetition do what argument alone cannot.
verses.reflection: Rest one minute in what cannot be cut, burned, wetted, or dried — it is reading these words.

verses.hook: Why is the self beyond all harm and change?

views.text: Each epithet follows from the one before: eternal, therefore everywhere; everywhere, therefore fixed; fixed, therefore unmoving; hence never produced anew. The repetition is deliberate, so that the hard-to-grasp Self may somehow come within reach of the intellect.

Gives a reason for each 'cannot': partless, so it cannot be cut or wetted; formless, so it cannot be burnt; not liquid, so it cannot be dried. Sthāṇu means it never turns into another form, acala that it never leaves its own.
Krishna repeats the soul's immortality on purpose; a good teacher restates key truths so they sink deep into the student's heart.

तस्मादेवं विदित्वैनं नानुशोचितुमर्हसि॥

avyakto'yamacintyo'yamavikāryo'yamucyate
tasmādevaṃ viditvainaṃ nānuśocitumarhasi
verses.essence: Unmanifest, unthinkable, unchangeable — so it is called. Knowing it thus, you have no cause to grieve.
verses.translation: This (Self) is said to be unmanifested, unthinkable and unchangeable. Therefore, knowing This to be such, thou shouldst not grieve.

anvaya.form: gerundive with negative prefix, masculine nominative singular (cannot be …)

verses.explanation: Three final negations close the description: avyakta — the senses cannot display it; acintya — the mind cannot model it; avikārya — change cannot occur in it. Krishna is honest about the limits of his own discourse: the self cannot be captured by the very instruments now hearing about it, since eye and thought only handle objects, and this is the subject. 'Knowing it thus' therefore means something subtle — knowing it as the unknowable knower. And from that, the refrain sounds for the first time in this run of verses: nānuśocitum arhasi — it does not befit you to grieve. It will return in 2.26, 2.27 and 2.30.
verses.connection: Concludes the portrait begun at 2.17 by sealing off the last exits — sense, thought, change — and converts the whole portrait into a verdict on grief.
verses.reflection: Stop grieving today for one thing the grief cannot reach, and feel the energy return.

verses.hook: Why can't the self be seen or grasped by thought?

refs.note: Beyond the senses are their objects, then the mind, then the intellect, and beyond the intellect is the soul.

views.text: Unmanifest because no sense can make it an object; unthinkable because only what the senses grasp becomes an object of thought; unchangeable because, having no parts, it cannot alter as milk turns to curd.
As pure consciousness without support or parts, it cannot be destroyed in any way. Passing to a new body is nothing new for it either: even in one life the body is never the same for a moment.
Takes the three words as beyond the eye and other senses, beyond the mind, and beyond the organs of action; 'ucyate', 'it is said', appeals to the testimony of those who know.
The soul is beyond the reach of eyes and intellect, which grasp only matter, so knowledge of the self must come from scripture and the guru.

verses.devanagari:
अथ चैनं नित्यजातं नित्यं वा मन्यसे मृतम् ।
तथापि त्वं महाबाहो नैवं शोचितुमर्हसि॥
verses.transliteration:
atha cainaṃ nityajātaṃ nityaṃ vā manyase mṛtam
tathāpi tvaṃ mahābāho naivaṃ śocitumarhasi
verses.essence: And even if you think it constantly born and constantly dying — even then, mighty-armed one, you ought not grieve.
verses.translation: But even if thou thinkest of It as being constantly born and constantly dying, even then, O mighty-armed, thou shouldst not grieve.

anvaya.meaning: but if, on the other hand

anvaya.parts: नित्य (constantly) + जात (born): 'born again and again'

anvaya.form: adjective, neuter accusative singular used as adverb

anvaya.parts: महा (great) + बाहु (arm): 'one whose arms are mighty'

verses.explanation: A startling move for a scripture: Krishna momentarily *grants the opposite worldview*. Suppose there is no eternal self — suppose beings really are just born and really do just die, the materialist's universe. Even then, he says, your collapse does not follow. The teaching refuses to rest its whole weight on one metaphysical pillar; it will now argue from inside the skeptic's own premises. A teacher confident enough to arm the opposing view is a teacher aiming at something deeper than doctrine — at the structure of grief itself.
verses.connection: Anticipates Arjuna's possible unbelief in 2.12–25 and opens a second front: the argument from inevitability.
verses.reflection: Even by the bleakest worldview, your despair is optional — test your sorrow against its own logic.

verses.hook: Even if the self were born and died again, should you grieve?

views.text: Spoken on the assumption, following ordinary experience, that the Self is born and dies with each body; even then grief is wrong, since what is born must die and what dies must be born.
The concession is to the view that the self is simply the body. Even then grief is out of place, because birth and death are the inevitable nature of a body, which is by nature subject to change.
Covers rival philosophies too: if beings are an unbroken stream of births, or, as the doctrine of momentary decay holds, are dying every instant, a rational person still has no ground for lament.
Grants for argument that the self is born and dies with each body, since the merit and demerit whose fruits are birth and death belong to it; even so, grief is not fitting.
Krishna addresses other philosophies, such as the Buddhist view of a self renewed each life, and says that even on that view there is no reason to lament.

verses.devanagari:
जातस्य हि ध्रुवो मृत्युर्ध्रुवं जन्म मृतस्य च ।

jātasya hi dhruvo mṛtyurdhruvaṃ janma mṛtasya ca
tasmādaparihārye'rthe na tvaṃ śocitumarhasi
verses.essence: For the born, death is certain; for the dead, birth is certain. Therefore, over the unavoidable, you should not grieve.
verses.translation: For certain is death for the born, and certain is birth for the dead; therefore, over the inevitable thou shouldst not grieve.

anvaya.form: pronoun, ablative singular used as adverb (from that = therefore)
gerundive with negative prefix, masculine locative singular (in/about)
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + परिहार्य (to be avoided): 'that cannot be avoided'

verses.explanation: The skeptic's-premise argument completes itself with two symmetries: born→death, certain; dead→birth, certain. The hinge word is aparihārya — that which cannot be averted by any effort whatsoever. Grief makes an implicit claim: *this should not be happening*. Against the genuinely unavoidable, that claim is incoherent — sorrow aimed at a law of nature is sorrow aimed at nothing. This is not coldness; it is the surgical separation of pain (inevitable) from the added torment of protesting the inevitable (optional). Bhishma and Drona, being born, were always already going to die; the only open question was the manner. Accepting the frame is what frees feeling to be clean inside it.
verses.connection: Completes 2.26: even granting that beings simply die, mourning the unavoidable is a category mistake.
verses.reflection: Accept one inevitability today fully — and watch how much fight in you was spent denying it.

verses.hook: Why grieve over a death that cannot be avoided?

refs.note: Yudhishthira tells the Yaksha that the greatest wonder is that people see others die daily yet think they themselves will live on.
Names the instinctive clinging to life, abhiniveśa, as a trait of the material intellect.

views.text: Death is certain for the born, without exception, and rebirth for the dead; since this pair is inevitable, there is no ground for grieving over a fact that cannot be avoided.

Origin and destruction are only successive states of something that already exists, as clay becomes lump, jar, shards and powder; the end of one state is the birth of the next, so there is nothing to grieve.
Death comes when the karma that began a body is used up, and rebirth follows from the karma done in it; both are fixed, so a wise man does not grieve over them.
Death is the one certainty for all who are born, so a wise person does not lament over what cannot be avoided.

verses.devanagari:
अव्यक्तादीनि भूतानि व्यक्तमध्यानि भारत ।
अव्यक्तनिधनान्येव तत्र का परिदेवना॥
verses.transliteration:
avyaktādīni bhūtāni vyaktamadhyāni bhārata
avyaktanidhanānyeva tatra kā paridevanā
verses.essence: Beings are unmanifest in their beginnings, manifest in the middle, unmanifest again in their ends. What is there to lament?
verses.translation: Beings are unmanifested in their beginning, manifested in their middle state, O Arjuna, and unmanifested again in their end. What is there to grieve about?

anvaya.parts: अव्यक्त (unmanifest) + आदि (beginning): 'having the unmanifest as their beginning'
व्यक्त (manifest) + मध्य (middle): 'whose middle is manifest'
अव्यक्त (unmanifest) + निधन (end): 'whose end is the unmanifest'

verses.explanation: A wide, almost cosmological camera angle: every being is a brief visibility between two invisibilities. Before birth — unmanifest; after death — unmanifest; the 'middle' that we call a life is the only segment the senses ever report. We grieve as if the manifest stretch were the whole of the person and its end an annihilation; but if both shores are unseen, death returns a being to the same mystery it came from. The question kā paridevanā — *what is there to mourn?* — is gentler than it sounds: it asks whether we have ever actually seen the thing we believe was destroyed.
verses.connection: Reframes 2.27's inevitability spatially: life as a window of manifestation, with the same unknown on either side.
verses.reflection: All beings emerge from mystery and return to it; let that soften your grip on the middle part.
verses.background: Krishna's first instruction begins. With the armies frozen around the chariot, he addresses the root of Arjuna's grief rather than its occasion: the deathless, unborn, all-pervading Self that weapons cannot cut — the wisdom called Sankhya, delivered to a warrior who believed he was about to commit murder.
verses.hook: Where are beings before birth and after death?

refs.note: Narada tells Yudhishthira that whether one sees a person as soul, body or both, there is no cause to grieve; only illusion-born attachment causes it.

views.text: Sons, friends and the rest came out of invisibility and return to it; they are not yours, nor you theirs. Citing the Mahabharata's Strī-parva, it calls grief over such passing appearances fruitless prattle.
Takes 'unmanifest' as primal nature, the causal state in which bodies already exist before they appear and into which they dissolve; grieving them is like grieving dream objects after waking.

Bodies and the relationships built on them meet and part like planks drifting in a river or pilgrims in an inn; what does not exist at the beginning and end should be seen as unreal in the middle too.
The soul exists in an unmanifest state with its subtle and causal bodies before birth and after death, and is manifest only in between, so death gives no reason for grief.

verses.devanagari:
आश्चर्यवत्पश्यति कश्चिदेन-
माश्चर्यवद्वदति तथैव चान्यः ।
आश्चर्यवच्चैनमन्यः शृणोति
श्रुत्वाप्येनं वेद न चैव कश्चित्॥
verses.transliteration:
āścaryavatpaśyati kaścidenam āścaryavadvadati tathaiva cānyaḥ
āścaryavaccainamanyaḥ śṛṇoti śrutvāpyenaṃ veda na caiva kaścit
verses.essence: One sees it as a wonder, another speaks of it as a wonder, another hears of it as a wonder — and even having heard, no one truly knows it.
verses.translation: One sees This (the Self) as a wonder; another speaks of It as a wonder; another hears of It as a wonder; yet having heard, none understands It at all.

anvaya.parts: आश्चर्य (wonder) + वत् (like): 'as if a wonder'
आश्चर्य (wonder) + वत् (like): 'as if a wonder'
आश्चर्य (wonder) + वत् (like): 'as if a wonder'

anvaya.form: verb, perfect form with present sense, 3rd person singular
indefinite pronoun, masculine nominative singular (with न: no one)

verses.explanation: After the dense argumentation, a sudden bow of humility — almost a sigh. The self is āścarya, a wonder, and the verse traces the whole chain of transmission: the rare one who sees, the one who can speak, the one who hears — and concedes that even hearing guarantees nothing. Krishna is describing this very conversation: he speaks as a wonder, Arjuna hears as a wonder, and understanding may still not dawn. Doctrine can be delivered; realization cannot. The verse protects the teaching from its own success — from the student who memorizes 'I am deathless' and mistakes the sentence for the seeing.
verses.connection: A pause for awe after 2.11–28: the truth just argued is not thereby transferred — knowledge of the self remains rare and wondrous.
verses.reflection: Approach the self today as a wonder, not a problem — astonishment is the correct first response.
verses.background: Krishna's first instruction begins. With the armies frozen around the chariot, he addresses the root of Arjuna's grief rather than its occasion: the deathless, unborn, all-pervading Self that weapons cannot cut — the wisdom called Sankhya, delivered to a warrior who believed he was about to commit murder.
verses.hook: Why do so few people truly understand the self, even after hearing about it?

refs.note: A realized teacher is rare, the chance to hear him rarer, and a student who understands rarest of all.

views.text: A wonder is something never seen before and suddenly met. Alternatively, the one who sees, speaks of or hears the Self is himself the wonder, rare among many thousands; either way, the Self is hard to know.
Only one in countless beings, purified by great austerity, sees the self; the 'and' implies that even among seers, speakers and hearers, one whose seeing, speaking and hearing are genuine is rare.
