The seer looks on as at a conjuror's trick, the truth seeming impossible because disbelief still overpowers him; another, held by contrary notions, hears and still does not know. This is why even learned people grieve.
As a fragment of God, the soul is wondrous and beyond intellect, so a true teacher is not discouraged when most people cannot grasp it.

verses.devanagari:
देही नित्यमवध्योऽयं देहे सर्वस्य भारत ।
तस्मात्सर्वाणि भूतानि न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि॥
verses.transliteration:
dehī nityamavadhyo'yaṃ dehe sarvasya bhārata
tasmātsarvāṇi bhūtāni na tvaṃ śocitumarhasi
verses.essence: The embodied one in everyone's body is forever beyond slaying, Bharata. Therefore you should not grieve for any being.
verses.translation: This, the Indweller in the body of everyone, is ever indestructible, O Arjuna; therefore, thou shouldst not grieve for any creature.

anvaya.base: देहिन् · one who has a body (the self)

anvaya.form: adjective, neuter accusative singular used as adverb
gerundive with negative prefix, masculine nominative singular (cannot be …)
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + वध्य (to be slain): 'unslayable'

anvaya.form: pronoun, ablative singular used as adverb (from that = therefore)
noun, neuter accusative plural (object: grieve for)

verses.explanation: The metaphysical movement closes with a summary stamped sarvasya — *in everyone*. Not only Bhishma and Drona: the deathless dweller is in every body on both sides of the field, in Duryodhana as much as in Yudhishthira. The refrain 'you should not grieve' sounds its fourth and last time in this section (after 2.25, 2.26 and 2.27), now extended to all beings everywhere. The teaching has reached its widest circumference — and precisely here Krishna will pivot, because Arjuna does not live at the widest circumference. He lives in a chariot, with a bow, and a duty. The next verse descends from eternity to that chariot.
verses.connection: Seals the section begun at 2.11. Grief has been answered at the level of being; the level of *doing* now opens.
verses.reflection: Walk through one hostile room remembering: nothing here can wound the dweller in this body.
verses.background: Krishna's first instruction begins. With the armies frozen around the chariot, he addresses the root of Arjuna's grief rather than its occasion: the deathless, unborn, all-pervading Self that weapons cannot cut — the wisdom called Sankhya, delivered to a warrior who believed he was about to commit murder.
verses.hook: Is there any being whose true self can be killed?

views.text: Being partless and all-pervasive, the self present in every body, even in trees, can never be killed; so there is no grief to be had for Bhishma or any of the others.
All selves, from gods down to plants, are alike in nature and eternal; inequality and perishing belong only to bodies, so grief is fit for no being at all, not just for Bhishma.
This verse sums up Krishna's teaching on the soul's immortality and its difference from the body.

verses.devanagari:
स्वधर्ममपि चावेक्ष्य न विकम्पितुमर्हसि ।
धर्म्याद्धि युद्धाच्छ्रेयोऽन्यत्क्षत्रियस्य न विद्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
svadharmamapi cāvekṣya na vikampitumarhasi
dharmyāddhi yuddhācchreyo'nyatkṣatriyasya na vidyate
verses.essence: And looking to your own dharma, you should not waver — for a kshatriya, nothing is higher than a righteous war.
verses.translation: Further, having regard to thy duty, shouldst not waver, for there is nothing higher for a Kshatriya than a righteous war.

anvaya.parts: स्व (own) + धर्म (duty): 'one's own duty'

anvaya.base: धर्म्य · in accord with dharma, righteous

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, neuter nominative singular

anvaya.base: क्षत्रिय · member of the warrior order

verses.explanation: The word svadharma enters the Gita — one's *own* dharma, the duty woven into one's station and nature — and the teaching changes registers from being to role. Arjuna is not a generic soul; he is a kshatriya, society's appointed protector, and this war (Krishna calls it dharmya, righteous — the qualifier matters) is precisely the contingency his entire existence was shaped for. The argument is no longer 'no one really dies' but 'this is yours to do.' A surgeon who faints at the sight of the one wound only she can close has not transcended her role; she has deserted it.
verses.connection: The pivot from 2.30: having dissolved death as a reason to mourn, Krishna takes up duty as a reason to act.
verses.reflection: Ask what your station in life uniquely obligates you to do — then stop negotiating with it.
verses.background: The teaching descends from metaphysics to station: Krishna reminds Arjuna of his own dharma as a kshatriya — the open door of righteous battle, the infamy of retreat, what his peers and enemies will say — and seals it with the verse of equanimity that makes fighting sinless.
verses.hook: Does Arjuna's own duty as a warrior also tell him to fight?

views.text: Fighting is the kshatriya's natural duty, and this battle is supremely righteous because it protects the people; to swerve from it is to swerve from what is natural to oneself.
Killing done as duty is compared to the animal offered in the Agnīṣomīya rite, which by scripture gains a better body, and to a surgeon's lancing: the act serves the good of the one it seems to harm.

Read as a direct answer to Arjuna's own words: his trembling body (1.29) and his 'I see no good in killing my kin' (1.31) are both answered by the claim that nothing is better for a kshatriya than a just war.
Duty has two levels: the soul's duty to love and serve God, and bodily duties by station and occupation; here Krishna appeals to Arjuna's bodily duty as a warrior to defend righteousness.

verses.devanagari:
यदृच्छया चोपपन्नं स्वर्गद्वारमपावृतम् ।
सुखिनः क्षत्रियाः पार्थ लभन्ते युद्धमीदृशम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yadṛcchayā copapannaṃ svargadvāramapāvṛtam
sukhinaḥ kṣatriyāḥ pārtha labhante yuddhamīdṛśam
verses.essence: Happy the kshatriyas, Partha, who find such a war — an open door to heaven, arrived unsought.
verses.translation: Happy are the Kshatriyas, O Arjuna! who are called upon to fight in such a battle that comes of itself as an open door to heaven.

anvaya.parts: स्वर्ग (heaven) + द्वार (door): 'the door of heaven'

anvaya.base: क्षत्रिय · member of the warrior order

verses.explanation: Krishna speaks for a moment in the pure idiom of the warrior code: a righteous war that arrives yadṛcchayā — unsought, by circumstance rather than ambition — is the kshatriya's rarest fortune, heaven's door standing open. The qualifier 'unsought' is load-bearing: Arjuna did not engineer this war; thirteen years of exile, an insulted queen, and every peace embassy refused brought it to his feet. He is not being asked to start a fire, only not to flee the one he is appointed to face. Within its own frame the argument is exact — and it is only scaffolding for the deeper architecture coming at 2.39.
verses.connection: Brightens 2.31: not merely permitted, the righteous fight is — within kshatriya-dharma — a privilege chance has handed him.
verses.reflection: Recognize one open door in your life right now that struggle disguised as misfortune.
verses.background: The teaching descends from metaphysics to station: Krishna reminds Arjuna of his own dharma as a kshatriya — the open door of righteous battle, the infamy of retreat, what his peers and enemies will say — and seals it with the verse of equanimity that makes fighting sinless.
verses.hook: Why should a warrior welcome a righteous war that comes unsought?

views.text: Answers why this battle is a duty: Kṣatriyas who meet such a war, arriving unsought (yadṛcchayā), are happy, for it stands as an open gate to heaven.
Even kshatriyas full of worldly desire should not avoid such a war, since it leads to heaven; how much less one who has just been taught this knowledge. The verse's point does not stop at heaven.
Also read as 'only those who get such a war are truly happy', which overturns Arjuna's earlier cry: how could we be happy after killing our own people?
Doing one's occupational duty brings virtuous rewards, not God-realization; the Gita calls for inner change while still acting, not for abandoning work.

verses.devanagari:
अथ चेत्त्वमिमं धर्म्यं संग्रामं न करिष्यसि ।
ततः स्वधर्मं कीर्तिं च हित्वा पापमवाप्स्यसि॥
verses.transliteration:
atha cettvamimaṃ dharmyaṃ saṃgrāmaṃ na kariṣyasi
tataḥ svadharmaṃ kīrtiṃ ca hitvā pāpamavāpsyasi
verses.essence: But if you will not wage this righteous war, then, abandoning your dharma and your honor, you will incur sin.
verses.translation: But if thou wilt not fight this righteous war, then having abandoned thine own duty and fame, thou shalt incur sin.

anvaya.base: धर्म्य · in accord with dharma, righteous

anvaya.parts: स्व (own) + धर्म (duty): 'one's own duty'

verses.explanation: The mirror argument: Arjuna has assumed that *fighting* is the sin and withdrawal the purity. Krishna inverts it — for the one person charged with protecting dharma, walking away *is* the sin, an abandonment (hitvā) of post. There is no neutral square on this board: the protector's inaction is itself an action, with consequences he will own. Pacifism is honorable for the renunciate who has left all stations; it is desertion for the soldier standing at his. Arjuna wanted to refuse the choice; Krishna shows him the refusal is also a choice, and the worse one.
verses.connection: The shadow of 2.32: the same dharma that makes the fight a privilege makes flight a transgression.
verses.reflection: Calculate honestly what avoiding your duty is already costing — avoidance has a price sheet too.
verses.background: The teaching descends from metaphysics to station: Krishna reminds Arjuna of his own dharma as a kshatriya — the open door of righteous battle, the infamy of retreat, what his peers and enemies will say — and seals it with the verse of equanimity that makes fighting sinless.
verses.hook: What happens if Arjuna refuses to fight this righteous war?

refs.note: A warrior's duty is to protect citizens, using force where needed, defeat enemy armies and rule by righteousness.

views.text: The fame at stake is specific: what Arjuna won by fighting Mahādeva (Śiva) and others; refusing a battle that scripture enjoins as duty forfeits that and brings only sin.
Withdrawal out of delusion loses two things — the immeasurable bliss that is the fruit of doing one's duty and the fame that comes with victory — and adds grave sin.
For a warrior on the battlefield, choosing non-violence is dereliction of duty and therefore a sin.

verses.devanagari:
अकीर्तिं चापि भूतानि कथयिष्यन्ति तेऽव्ययाम् ।
सम्भावितस्य चाकीर्तिर्मरणादतिरिच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
akīrtiṃ cāpi bhūtāni kathayiṣyanti te'vyayām
sambhāvitasya cākīrtirmaraṇādatiricyate
verses.essence: And people will recount your undying infamy — and for the honored, disgrace is worse than death.
verses.translation: People, too, will recount thy everlasting dishonour; and to one who has been honoured, dishonour is worse than death.

anvaya.form: verb, passive form, present, 3rd person singular

verses.explanation: Krishna descends another step, to the most human register: reputation. The world will not read Arjuna's heart; it will read his retreat, and tell of it forever — akīrti avyayā, an *imperishable* infamy, the dark twin of the imperishable self. The irony is deliberate: refuse the teaching about what cannot die, and you will acquire the other thing that cannot die. For a sambhāvita — one held high in honor — such disgrace outweighs death itself. This is not the Gita's loftiest argument and is not meant to be; a complete teacher addresses the whole man, including the part that cares what the world will say.
verses.connection: Extends 2.33 from inner sin to outer name: dharma abandoned has a social afterlife, and it does not fade.
verses.reflection: Care a little less today what the story says, and more what the deed actually was.
verses.background: The teaching descends from metaphysics to station: Krishna reminds Arjuna of his own dharma as a kshatriya — the open door of righteous battle, the infamy of retreat, what his peers and enemies will say — and seals it with the verse of equanimity that makes fighting sinless.
verses.hook: What would refusing to fight do to Arjuna's name?

views.text: Beyond losing his duty and fame, people will speak of his unending infamy; for one honoured as virtuous and heroic, death is preferable to infamy.

Everyone, worthy and unworthy alike, will mock him for all time with 'when the battle began, Arjuna ran away'; for one honoured for courage, such disgrace is worse than death, so death itself would be better.
If higher knowledge does not move Arjuna, Krishna appeals to a lower motive: for an honoured warrior, disgrace is worse than death.

verses.devanagari:
भयाद्रणादुपरतं मंस्यन्ते त्वां महारथाः ।
येषां च त्वं बहुमतो भूत्वा यास्यसि लाघवम्॥
verses.transliteration:
bhayādraṇāduparataṃ maṃsyante tvāṃ mahārathāḥ
yeṣāṃ ca tvaṃ bahumato bhūtvā yāsyasi lāghavam
verses.essence: The great warriors will think you fled the battle from fear — and you, whom they held in highest regard, will fall into their contempt.
verses.translation: The great car-warriors will think that thou hast withdrawn from the battle through fear; and thou wilt be lightly held by them who have thought much of thee.

anvaya.form: noun, neuter ablative singular (from, because of)

anvaya.parts: महा (great) + रथ (chariot): 'one whose chariot is great', a top-rank warrior
बहु (much) + मत (thought of): 'held in high regard'

anvaya.meaning: you will go to, fall into

verses.explanation: The cruelest precision: Arjuna believes his withdrawal would be read as compassion; Krishna names how it will actually be read — bhayāt, *from fear*. The mahārathas of the opposing army — Karna, Duryodhana, men who have envied his standing for decades — will never credit a crisis of conscience; cowardice is the only story they are equipped to tell. His weightiness (bahumata, much-esteemed) will turn to lāghava, lightness — the awful physics of reputation, where gravity once lost is not regained. The world cannot see motives; it can only see exits.
verses.connection: Sharpens 2.34 from anonymous report to named audience: the very peers whose regard built Arjuna will author his disgrace.
verses.reflection: The people who respect your strength are watching how you carry this — carry it upright.
verses.background: The teaching descends from metaphysics to station: Krishna reminds Arjuna of his own dharma as a kshatriya — the open door of righteous battle, the infamy of retreat, what his peers and enemies will say — and seals it with the verse of equanimity that makes fighting sinless.
verses.hook: What will the great warriors think if Arjuna leaves the battle?

views.text: Duryodhana and the other great chariot-warriors will think he quit the fight not from compassion but from fear of Karṇa and others, and he will fall into disgrace before those who once esteemed him.
To brave enemies, a hero never turns from battle out of love for kin; they can explain it only as fear. So Karna and Duryodhana, who once rated him a formidable foe, will think him easy to beat.
Warriors who respected Arjuna would not know his retreat came from love for his kin; they would think he fled in fear of them.

verses.devanagari:
अवाच्यवादांश्च बहून्वदिष्यन्ति तवाहिताः ।
निन्दन्तस्तव सामर्थ्यं ततो दुःखतरं नु किम्॥
verses.transliteration:
avācyavādāṃśca bahūnvadiṣyanti tavāhitāḥ
nindantastava sāmarthyaṃ tato duḥkhataraṃ nu kim
verses.essence: Your enemies will speak many unspeakable words, mocking your prowess. What could be more painful than that?
verses.translation: Thy enemies also, cavilling at thy power, will speak many abusive words. What is more painful than this?

anvaya.base: अवाच्य · not to be spoken + वाद · word, talk
anvaya.parts: अवाच्य (unspeakable) + वाद (words): 'words that should never be said'

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine nominative plural (while doing)

verses.explanation: The argument-from-honor reaches its floor: avācya-vādān, words that should not be spoken — taunts coarse beyond repeating — aimed precisely at his sāmarthya, the warrior's competence that is the core of his self-image. Krishna ends with a question rather than a claim: *you* tell me what is more painful. He is making Arjuna run the comparison himself — the imagined agony of fighting kin against the guaranteed agony of a lifetime of mockery. The honor arguments (2.33–36) now stand complete; whether or not they are the *highest* reasons, they are true predictions, and Arjuna knows it.
verses.connection: Bottom of the descent begun at 2.34: from history's verdict, to peers' contempt, to enemies' open mockery.
verses.reflection: Imagine your critics narrating your retreat; then act so their version becomes unwritable.
verses.background: The teaching descends from metaphysics to station: Krishna reminds Arjuna of his own dharma as a kshatriya — the open door of righteous battle, the infamy of retreat, what his peers and enemies will say — and seals it with the verse of equanimity that makes fighting sinless.
verses.hook: What would Arjuna's enemies say about him if he withdrew?

views.text: The might being scorned is concrete: the prowess Arjuna earned in battles against the Nivātakavaca demons and others; no sorrow is greater than being scorned for it.
Imagines the actual taunt of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons — 'how could Pārtha stand before heroes like us even a moment? His prowess is for elsewhere' — so that Arjuna sees death would be preferable.
If he fled, Arjuna's enemies would mock and vilify him with cruel words, and such derision would hurt him deeply.

verses.devanagari:
हतो वा प्राप्स्यसि स्वर्गं जित्वा वा भोक्ष्यसे महीम् ।
तस्मादुत्तिष्ठ कौन्तेय युद्धाय कृतनिश्चयः॥
verses.transliteration:
hato vā prāpsyasi svargaṃ jitvā vā bhokṣyase mahīm
tasmāduttiṣṭha kaunteya yuddhāya kṛtaniścayaḥ
verses.essence: Slain, you gain heaven; victorious, you enjoy the earth. Therefore arise, Kaunteya, resolved to fight.
verses.translation: Slain, thou wilt obtain heaven; victorious, thou wilt enjoy the earth; therefore, stand up, O son of Kunti, resolved to fight.

anvaya.form: pronoun, ablative singular used as adverb (from that = therefore)

anvaya.parts: कृत (made) + निश्चय (resolve): 'one who has made a firm resolve'

verses.explanation: The warrior-logic closes with a perfect dilemma turned inside out: Arjuna saw two losses (win and lose family, lose and lose all); Krishna shows two gains — death in righteous battle opens heaven, victory yields the earth. Within kshatriya-dharma the accounting is flawless: the downside has been deleted. And then the command repeats from 2.3 — uttiṣṭha, *stand up* — but now buttressed by every level of argument from metaphysics to honor to outcome. Note what Krishna has quietly done: met Arjuna's either/or despair with an either/or hope. The frame itself — acting *for* outcomes — still stands. The next verse will be the first crack in that frame.
verses.connection: Completes the conventional case begun at 2.31: by the warrior's own arithmetic, both branches of the battle now pay.
verses.reflection: Reframe one risk today as Krishna does: count what is gained in both outcomes, then move.
verses.background: The teaching descends from metaphysics to station: Krishna reminds Arjuna of his own dharma as a kshatriya — the open door of righteous battle, the infamy of retreat, what his peers and enemies will say — and seals it with the verse of equanimity that makes fighting sinless.
verses.hook: What does Arjuna stand to gain whether he wins or dies?

views.text: Either way Arjuna gains: killed, heaven; victorious over Karṇa and the rest, the earth. So he should rise with the resolve, 'I shall either defeat the enemies or die.'
Duty fought without attachment to its fruit becomes the means to supreme bliss, so the 'heaven' of the slain points beyond itself: Arjuna is to rise knowing that fighting is a means to release.
Verses 2.33–37 are argued from the opponent's own ground: even if Arjuna prefers to go by generally accepted practice, the fight must still be undertaken.
Answers Arjuna's doubt in 2.6, 'we do not know which is better, that we win or that they win': in either case he gains.

verses.devanagari:
सुखदुःखे समे कृत्वा लाभालाभौ जयाजयौ ।
ततो युद्धाय युज्यस्व नैवं पापमवाप्स्यसि॥
verses.transliteration:
sukhaduḥkhe same kṛtvā lābhālābhau jayājayau
tato yuddhāya yujyasva naivaṃ pāpamavāpsyasi
verses.essence: Holding pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal — then join the battle. Thus you will incur no sin.
verses.translation: Having made pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat the same, engage thou in battle for the sake of battle; thus thou shalt not incur sin.

anvaya.form: noun (compound), neuter accusative dual (the pair, as object)
anvaya.parts: सुख (pleasure) + दुःख (pain): 'pleasure and pain', a pair

anvaya.form: noun (compound), masculine accusative dual (the pair, as object)
anvaya.parts: लाभ (gain) + अलाभ (non-gain): 'gain and loss'

anvaya.form: noun (compound), masculine accusative dual (the pair, as object)
anvaya.parts: जय (victory) + अजय (non-victory): 'victory and defeat'

anvaya.form: imperative, 2nd person singular, middle voice (a command)

verses.explanation: In one verse, the door to everything that follows. Until now: fight, because heaven or earth will pay you (2.37). Suddenly: make the payments *equal* — same kṛtvā — pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat — and *then* fight. The motivational engine of 2.37 is dismantled one verse after it was built. What remains when outcomes no longer drive the act? Duty performed because it is one's own, with the result released in advance. And here is the answer to Arjuna's deepest terror — sin: it is not the act that binds, but the craving wound into it. An act done in equanimity, Krishna says, incurs no sin. The word yujyasva — *yoke yourself* — plants the seed of 'yoga' one verse before its formal arrival.
verses.connection: The hinge of the chapter: outcome-logic (2.31–37) is suddenly transcended, preparing the explicit turn to buddhi-yoga in 2.39.
verses.reflection: Before your next contest, vow: equal in win and loss — then enter, and watch fear shrink.
verses.background: The teaching descends from metaphysics to station: Krishna reminds Arjuna of his own dharma as a kshatriya — the open door of righteous battle, the infamy of retreat, what his peers and enemies will say — and seals it with the verse of equanimity that makes fighting sinless.
verses.hook: How can you fight a hard battle without being stained by sin?

refs.note: Good deeds lead to heaven, bad deeds to lower realms, mixed deeds back to earth; all such selfish action binds, which is why acting without attachment frees.

views.text: The advice to fight is incidental: the real subject since 2.12 is knowledge of the supreme Reality, and fighting is mentioned only as Arjuna's natural duty, not as a call to combine knowledge with action.
'Sin' here means the bondage of transmigration: fighting with knowledge of the self, unmoved by wounds, gain or loss, and free of desire even for heaven, releases one from it.

Answers Arjuna's 'sin alone will take hold of us' (1.36), and reads the pairs as a chain: pleasure and pain come from gain and loss, which come from victory and defeat; evenness means freedom from elation and dejection.

Selfish motives create karmic reactions, even for good deeds. Work done as duty to God, with equal regard for victory and defeat, creates no reaction, just as a soldier on duty is not punished for killing.

verses.devanagari:
एषा तेऽभिहिता साङ्ख्ये बुद्धिर्योगे त्विमां शृणु ।
बुद्ध्या युक्तो यया पार्थ कर्मबन्धं प्रहास्यसि॥
verses.transliteration:
eṣā te'bhihitā sāṅkhye buddhiryoge tvimāṃ śṛṇu
buddhyā yukto yayā pārtha karmabandhaṃ prahāsyasi
verses.essence: This wisdom of Sankhya has been declared to you; now hear it in Yoga — yoked to which, Partha, you will cast off the bondage of karma.
verses.translation: This, which has been taught to thee, is wisdom concerning Sankhya. Now listen to wisdom concerning Yoga, endowed with which, O Arjuna, thou shalt cast off the bonds of action.

anvaya.form: pronoun, dative singular (to you), short form
relative pronoun, feminine instrumental singular (with which)

anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + बन्ध (bond): 'the bondage caused by action'

verses.explanation: Krishna names what he has done and what he is about to do. Everything from 2.11 to 2.30 was sāṅkhya — the discriminative knowledge of what is real. Now comes yoga — the same wisdom turned into a *method*, a way of acting. The promise is precise: karma-bandhaṁ prahāsyasi, you will shed the bondage of action. This is the exact answer to Arjuna's paralysis, for his real fear was never battle but *bondage* — that action would chain him to sin. Krishna's reply: action does not bind; acting *for the fruit* binds. There exists a way of doing in which the doing leaves no residue. The rest of the Gita is the unfolding of this single sentence.
verses.connection: Names the transition that 2.38 enacted: from knowing the deathless self to a discipline of unbound action.
verses.reflection: You have understood enough theory; ask now for the discipline that makes understanding walk.
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: After knowledge of the self, what second teaching does Krishna now offer?

views.text: Sankhya is the knowledge of supreme Reality that removes ignorance; yoga is the means to it — detached action offered to God, and meditation. The bondage of merit and demerit falls away when knowledge comes by God's grace.
Sankhya is the truth about the self that the intellect grasps, taught in 2.12–30; yoga is the mental attitude needed for works done with that knowledge, which together become the means to release.
The same determinate knowledge serves both, yoga meaning skill in action. Actions are insentient and cannot bind; it is the self that binds itself through actions in the form of mental impressions.

Having taught analytical knowledge of the soul, Krishna turns to the yoga of the intellect: working without desire for rewards, where a discerning intellect detaches the mind from the fruits of action.

verses.devanagari:
नेहाभिक्रमनाशोऽस्ति प्रत्यवायो न विद्यते ।
स्वल्पमप्यस्य धर्मस्य त्रायते महतो भयात्॥
verses.transliteration:
nehābhikramanāśo'sti pratyavāyo na vidyate
svalpamapyasya dharmasya trāyate mahato bhayāt
verses.essence: In this path no effort is lost, no reversal occurs. Even a little of this dharma rescues from great fear.
verses.translation: In this there is no loss of effort, nor is there any harm (production of contrary results or transgression). Even a little of this knowledge (even a little practice of this Yoga) protects one from great fear.

anvaya.parts: अभिक्रम (a beginning, effort) + नाश (loss): 'the loss of an effort once begun'

verses.explanation: Before teaching the method, Krishna posts its guarantee — written against the two fine-print clauses of ritual and worldly work, where a rite abandoned midway is wasted (abhikrama-nāśa) and a rite done wrong backfires (pratyavāya). Karma-yoga has neither clause. Every step counts; no step harms; there is no wrong way to begin and no penalty for imperfection. Svalpam api — even a sliver — protects from mahato bhayāt, the great fear: the dread of the round of birth and death, the very dread Arjuna is drowning in at this moment. It is the most encouraging sentence in the chapter: this path cannot be failed, only paused, and every attempt is banked.
verses.connection: Underwrites the new path of 2.39: unlike ritual religion, this yoga is risk-free and cumulative — every attempt is banked.
verses.reflection: Begin the smallest practice today knowing it cannot be wasted — this path keeps every deposit.
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: Is any effort on the spiritual path ever wasted or lost?

refs.note: Human birth is a rare chance; whoever fails to use it for the highest goal meets great ruin.
Without striving for God-realization in this life, one keeps wandering through countless species of life, birth after birth.

views.text: On the path of action toward Liberation no beginning is wasted, unlike farming, and no harm follows, unlike medical treatment; even a little of this Yoga saves one from the great fear of birth and death.

In unselfish work an effort left unfinished is not fruitless and brings no evil, unlike Vedic or worldly works done for results; the same promise returns in 6.40. The great fear is that of transmigration.
Since no negligence is possible in this knowledge, there is no loss through lapse; a little of it ends the great danger of rebirth, as a little sandal cools a cauldron of boiling oil.
Because the work is done for the Lord alone, obstacles and faulty performance cannot spoil it; even the bare beginning of it saves from samsara, unlike rites for desired ends that fail with one flaw.
The great danger is losing human birth in the next life. Material gains are left at death, but God preserves every bit of spiritual progress and lets one resume from where one left off.

verses.devanagari:
व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिरेकेह कुरुनन्दन ।
बहुशाखा ह्यनन्ताश्च बुद्धयोऽव्यवसायिनाम्॥
verses.transliteration:
vyavasāyātmikā buddhirekeha kurunandana
bahuśākhā hyanantāśca buddhayo'vyavasāyinām
verses.essence: Here the resolute understanding is one, Kurunandana. Many-branched and endless are the thoughts of the irresolute.
verses.translation: Here, O joy of the Kurus, there is but a single one-pointed determination; many-branched and endless are the thoughts of the irresolute.

anvaya.base: व्यवसायात्मक · having resolve as its nature
anvaya.parts: व्यवसाय (resolve, determination) + आत्मक (having the nature of): whose nature is resolve

anvaya.base: कुरुनन्दन · delight of the Kuru line
anvaya.parts: कुरु (the Kuru dynasty) + नन्दन (joy, son): joy of the Kurus
बहु (many) + शाखा (branch): having many branches
अन् (not) + अन्त (end): having no end

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, genitive plural (of)
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + व्यवसायिन् (resolute): those without resolve

verses.explanation: The first technical requirement: vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ — an understanding with the nature of settled resolve, gathered to a single point. Its opposite is drawn from Arjuna's own state: thoughts bahu-śākhāḥ, many-branched — duty pointing one way, love another, fear of sin a third, fear of shame a fourth — an inner committee in permanent session. The mind fragmented across aims cannot act cleanly; the mind unified can. Karma-yoga's first gift is the collapse of the committee: one criterion (is this mine to do?) replaces the endless audit of outcomes. Singleness, not cleverness, is the entry fee.
verses.connection: Begins specifying the buddhi of 2.39: before all else, it must be *one* — the precise cure for the branching paralysis of chapter 1.
verses.reflection: Gather your scattered wantings for one hour behind a single resolve, and feel the power of one.
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: What sets a resolute mind apart from a scattered one?

views.text: Takes iha as the path to liberation. The one-pointed conviction comes from a valid source of knowledge and cancels the branching contrary notions; those many-branched thoughts keep worldly existence endless until right knowledge ends them.

For a seeker of release every scriptural rite serves one fruit, liberation, so the resolute mind about them is single, as several sacrifices form one injunction for one result. The desire-driven mind splits by the many fruits it chases.
Determination as such is one and natural to everyone; it only appears manifold because of the many objects it is directed toward.
Iha means karma-yoga as worship of the Lord, where the resolve is 'by devotion to the Supreme alone I shall surely cross'. Desires are endless, so the minds of the desirous branch without end.

The intellect governs the mind's desires. When it firmly decides that all work is for God's pleasure, the aspirant moves toward the goal like an arrow; a many-branched intellect lets the mind run everywhere.

verses.devanagari:
यामिमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्यविपश्चितः ।
वेदवादरताः पार्थ नान्यदस्तीति वादिनः॥
verses.transliteration:
yāmimāṃ puṣpitāṃ vācaṃ pravadantyavipaścitaḥ
vedavādaratāḥ pārtha nānyadastīti vādinaḥ
verses.essence: The undiscerning, delighting in the letter of the Veda, Partha, utter flowery speech, declaring: there is nothing else.
verses.translation: Flowery speech is uttered by the unwise, taking pleasure in the eulogising words of the Vedas, O Arjuna, saying, "There is nothing else."

anvaya.form: past participle used as adjective, feminine, accusative singular

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + विपश्चित् (wise, discerning): the unwise

anvaya.base: वेदवादरत · devoted to the Veda's statements
anvaya.parts: वेद (Veda) + वाद (statement, eulogy) + रत (delighting in): who delight in the Veda's promises

verses.explanation: Now the chief enemy of one-pointedness is named, and the target is audacious: not vice, but a certain *religion*. The avipaścitaḥ — undiscerning — who delight in veda-vāda, the letter of scripture, preaching puṣpitā vāc, blossoming speech: gorgeous ritual promises of heaven, cattle, sons, rain. Their creed is nānyad asti — 'there is nothing else,' nothing beyond the marketplace of rites and rewards. Krishna's point is not anti-Veda (he will honor it at 2.46) but anti-reduction: when religion becomes a transaction catalogue, it multiplies desires instead of dissolving them — and a desire multiplied is a mind branched.
verses.connection: Diagnoses the social source of the many-branched mind of 2.41: an entire religious culture organized around desirable fruits.
verses.reflection: Notice the flowery promises you still believe — the ones that keep you shopping instead of arriving.
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: Who are the people dazzled by the flowery promises of ritual?

refs.note: Those performing showy rituals for heavenly pleasures think themselves learned but are fools, like the blind leading the blind.

views.text: The speech is flowery like a tree in bloom: pleasant to hear and seemingly meaningful, though only words revealing the Self truly are. 'Nothing else' means no God or liberation beyond rites that win heaven.

Puṣpitā is like a poison creeper, lovely only at first sight. Veda-vāda means the arthavāda praise-passages, such as 'we drank soma and became immortal'; their creed denies any reality of the Lord beyond them.

Identifies these people with the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā stress on the ritual portion of the Veda, and reminds the reader that heaven itself is transitory: one returns when merit is spent, and only Self-knowledge frees.

The ritual section of the Vedas offers material rewards and heaven, and pleasure-seekers glorify it. Heaven is still inside the material world, so one returns from it; the wise do not make even heaven their goal.

verses.devanagari:
कामात्मानः स्वर्गपरा जन्मकर्मफलप्रदाम् ।
क्रियाविशेषबहुलां भोगैश्वर्यगतिं प्रति॥
verses.transliteration:
kāmātmānaḥ svargaparā janmakarmaphalapradām
kriyāviśeṣabahulāṃ bhogaiśvaryagatiṃ prati
verses.essence: Souls of desire, bent on heaven, they offer speech rich in rites that yield birth as the fruit of works — aimed at enjoyment and power.
verses.translation: Full of desires, having heaven as their goal, (they utter speech which is directed to ends) leading to new births as the result of their works, and prescribe various methods abounding in specific actions, for the attainment of pleasure and power.

anvaya.parts: काम (desire) + आत्मन् (self, nature): whose very nature is desire
स्वर्ग (heaven) + पर (highest goal): for whom heaven is supreme

anvaya.meaning: offering birth as fruit of action
anvaya.base: जन्मकर्मफलप्रद · granting birth as the result of deeds
anvaya.form: adjective, feminine, accusative singular (qualifies the speech)
anvaya.parts: जन्म (birth) + कर्म (action) + फल (fruit) + प्रद (giving): which offers birth as the fruit of action
क्रिया (rite) + विशेष (particular) + बहुल (abounding): abounding in particular rites

anvaya.base: भोगैश्वर्यगति · the reaching of pleasure and lordship
anvaya.form: noun, feminine, accusative singular (object of प्रति)
anvaya.parts: भोग (enjoyment) + ऐश्वर्य (lordship, power) + गति (attainment): the attaining of enjoyment and power

verses.explanation: The portrait sharpens into a single devastating compound: kāmātmānaḥ — those whose *self is made of desire*, identity and craving fused. Their ceiling is svarga, heaven imagined as pleasure perfected; their instrument, an abundance of special rites; their actual harvest — and here is Krishna's quiet bombshell — janma, *rebirth*. The ritual economy they trust does not free its customers; it recycles them. Even its successes return as new bodies with new appetites. A heaven that is the fruit of works is, by that very fact, temporary — spiritual interest payments, never the principal.
verses.connection: Continues 2.42: behind the flowery speech, a psychology (desire-as-self) and its inescapable revolving door (rebirth).
verses.reflection: Trace one desire to its actual destination: is it a place, or just a better-decorated wheel?
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: What do people seek when they make heaven and pleasure their goal?

refs.note: Those performing showy rituals for heavenly pleasures think themselves learned but are fools, like the blind leading the blind.

views.text: Reads janma-karma-phala-pradā as speech that promises birth itself as the fruit of rites; those who proclaim it keep moving in the cycle of transmigration.
Heaven is only a pause: after it comes rebirth, which offers the chance to perform more rites without true knowledge, aimed again at pleasure and power.
Splits the compound three ways: the speech grants birth, the actions to be done in that birth, and their fruits — a self-renewing round.
Striving for the celestial abodes through ritual keeps one in the cycle of birth and death, because heavenly pleasures end when merit runs out. Spiritual wisdom looks beyond them to God-realization.

verses.devanagari:
भोगैश्वर्यप्रसक्तानां तयापहृतचेतसाम् ।
व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिः समाधौ न विधीयते॥
verses.transliteration:
bhogaiśvaryaprasaktānāṃ tayāpahṛtacetasām
vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ samādhau na vidhīyate
verses.essence: For those clinging to enjoyment and power, their minds carried off by that speech, the resolute understanding does not arise in samadhi.
verses.translation: For those who are attached to pleasure and power, whose minds are drawn away by such teaching, that determinate reason is not formed which is steadily bent on meditation and Samadhi (superconscious state).

anvaya.meaning: of those attached to pleasure and power
anvaya.base: भोगैश्वर्यप्रसक्त · clinging to enjoyment and lordship
anvaya.parts: भोग (enjoyment) + ऐश्वर्य (power) + प्रसक्त (deeply attached): deeply attached to enjoyment and power

anvaya.base: अपहृतचेतस् · one whose mind is stolen
anvaya.parts: अपहृत (carried away, from अप + √हृ) + चेतस् (mind): those whose minds are carried away

anvaya.base: व्यवसायात्मक · having resolve as its nature
anvaya.parts: व्यवसाय (resolve) + आत्मक (having the nature of): whose nature is resolve

anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is set)

verses.explanation: The indictment closes by naming the casualty. Apahṛta-cetasām — minds *stolen*, carried off like plunder by beautiful promises. And what the theft prevents: vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ... samādhau — the one-pointed understanding can find no footing in samādhi, the settled depth of the mind. The sequence is mechanical, not moralistic: attachment to outcomes → mind hijacked by whatever advertises outcomes → no inner stillness possible. Arjuna can now see his own chapter-one collapse in this mirror: a mind seized by imagined fruits (kingdom, sin, family ruin) and therefore incapable of standing in one place.
verses.connection: Completes the arc 2.41–44: why the many-branched mind happens — fruit-fixation steals the very faculty that yoga requires.
verses.reflection: Find what your attachments have made you unable to sit still for — there is your homework.
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: Why can't someone chasing pleasure and wealth hold a firm resolve?

views.text: Samādhi here means the mind, 'that into which everything is gathered' for a person's experience; na vidhīyate means the one-pointed conviction simply does not arise in it, because discrimination is covered over.
Such minds cannot form the resolve that sees every Vedic rite as a means to liberation, founded on knowing the self; so a seeker must not cling to rites as mere tools of desire.
Such people may even have determinate knowledge, yet are unfit for concentration, because they never settle on concentration itself as the fruit to seek.
Samādhi is the mind's one-pointedness turned toward the Supreme Lord. Vidhīyate is a passive used in an active sense: the resolute understanding does not arise there.
Those attached to enjoyment and luxury spend their intellect planning how to earn and enjoy more, and so they never develop the firm resolve that the path to God requires.

verses.devanagari:
त्रैगुण्यविषया वेदा निस्त्रैगुण्यो भवार्जुन ।
निर्द्वन्द्वो नित्यसत्त्वस्थो निर्योगक्षेम आत्मवान्॥
verses.transliteration:
traiguṇyaviṣayā vedā nistraiguṇyo bhavārjuna
nirdvandvo nityasattvastho niryogakṣema ātmavān
verses.essence: The Vedas deal with the three gunas — be beyond the three gunas, Arjuna: free of the pairs, ever in sattva, beyond acquiring and keeping, established in the Self.
verses.translation: The Vedas deal with the three attributes (of Nature); be thou above these three attributes. O Arjuna, free yourself from the pairs of opposites, and ever remain in the quality of Sattva (goodness), freed from (the thought of) acquisition and preservation, and be established in the Self.

anvaya.base: त्रैगुण्यविषय · having the three guṇas as subject
anvaya.parts: त्रैगुण्य (the triad of guṇas) + विषय (scope, subject matter): whose subject is the three guṇas

anvaya.base: निस्त्रैगुण्य · free of the three guṇas
anvaya.parts: निस् (without, beyond) + त्रैगुण्य (the three guṇas): free of the three guṇas

anvaya.meaning: free of the pairs of opposites
anvaya.parts: निर् (without) + द्वन्द्व (pair of opposites): free from heat-cold, pleasure-pain
नित्य (always) + सत्त्व (sattva, clarity) + स्थ (standing in): ever standing in sattva

anvaya.base: निर्योगक्षेम · without care for acquisition and preservation
anvaya.parts: निर् (without) + योग (getting what one lacks) + क्षेम (keeping what one has)

anvaya.base: आत्मवत् · possessed of the self, self-collected

verses.explanation: The boldest sentence yet: the Vedas themselves operate within traiguṇya — the three strands of nature, sattva, rajas, tamas, the whole machinery of the conditioned world — and Arjuna is told to step *beyond* the machinery: nistraiguṇyo bhava. Then four marks of the one who has: free of the dvandvas, the pairs (hot-cold, gain-loss) that whipsaw the mind; resting in steady clarity; nir-yogakṣema — released from the two anxieties that run ordinary life, *getting* what one lacks and *guarding* what one has; and ātmavān, self-possessed in the deepest sense. It is a portrait of the unhooked human being.
verses.connection: Raises 2.42–44 to its conclusion: not merely avoid bad religion — outgrow the entire fruit-bearing order the rites belong to.
verses.reflection: Step outside one pair of opposites today — gain-loss, praise-blame — and breathe the unpaired air.
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: Why does Krishna tell Arjuna to rise above the Vedas' three qualities?

views.text: Traiguṇya means worldly life, the sum of virtuous, vicious and mixed acts and their results. Since Arjuna is also told to stay in sattva, nistraiguṇya must mean free from desire; ātmavān means vigilant.

The Vedas, out of love, teach people dominated by each guṇa the means to what they want. Arjuna should instead increase pure sattva alone, and drop getting and keeping anything not needed for knowing the self.

The Vedas bind only through the guṇas, when rites are done for pleasure, to avoid pain or from attachment; they do not bind by themselves. The verse cannot be condemning the Veda, or the duty to fight would fall with it.

The Vedas give ritual rewards to lift worldly people gradually from ignorance to goodness. Krishna is not rejecting the Vedas but telling Arjun not to be drawn by their reward-seeking section, and to use their divine knowledge instead.

verses.devanagari:
यावानर्थ उदपाने सर्वतः सम्प्लुतोदके ।
तावान्सर्वेषु वेदेषु ब्राह्मणस्य विजानतः॥
verses.transliteration:
yāvānartha udapāne sarvataḥ samplutodake
tāvānsarveṣu vedeṣu brāhmaṇasya vijānataḥ
verses.essence: As much use as a well when water floods on every side — that much use are all the Vedas to a brahmana who knows.
verses.translation: To the Brahmana who has known the Self, all the Vedas are of as much use as is a reservoir of water in a place where there is a flood.

anvaya.parts: उद (water) + पान (drinking): a place to drink water
सम्प्लुत (flooded) + उदक (water): where water has overflowed

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, genitive singular (of one knowing)

verses.explanation: A flood-image resolves the tension of the last four verses with perfect courtesy. A well is not condemned when the flood comes — it was real water, honestly useful, in the time of scarcity. But to a man standing in water to the horizon, the well is simply *included*. So with the rites and rewards of scripture for the vijānat, the one who knows: nothing is denounced, everything is exceeded. Every finite goal the rituals offer is contained in the infinite the knower stands in. This is how the Gita transcends — never by burning the ladder, only by reaching the roof.
verses.connection: The peace treaty after 2.42–45: ritual religion is not false but small — a well honored, then engulfed, by the flood of knowledge.
verses.reflection: Once the flood is everywhere, stop guarding your old buckets; let a smaller method retire gracefully.
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: What use are the scriptures to someone who has realized the truth?

refs.note: All Vedic mantras, rituals, practices, knowledge and duties have one aim: to bring the soul to God.
Krishna tells Uddhav that those who grasp the Vedas' purpose and set aside lesser duties to serve him wholeheartedly are the highest devotees.

views.text: Every use of small ponds is met in a flood; so every result of Vedic rites is contained in the knower's realization, as the Chāndogya says of Raikva. Until one is fit for knowledge, rites still have to be done.
A thirsty man takes only what he can drink from a vast reservoir built for many uses; so the knowing seeker takes from the Vedas only what serves release, not everything in them.
The Vedas' many rituals and their material allurements all serve one aim, uniting the soul with God. Whoever attaches the mind to God already fulfills the purpose of every Vedic instruction.

verses.devanagari:
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन ।
मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि॥
verses.transliteration:
karmaṇyevādhikāraste mā phaleṣu kadācana
mā karmaphalaheturbhūrmā te saṅgo'stvakarmaṇi
verses.essence: Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits. Be not the author of the fruits of action; be not attached to inaction.
verses.translation: Thy right is to work only, but never with its fruits; let not the fruits of action be thy motive, nor let thy attachment be to inaction.

anvaya.meaning: driven by (or cause of) action's fruit
anvaya.base: कर्मफलहेतु · one whose motive is the fruit of action
anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + फल (fruit) + हेतु (motive, cause): one whose motive is the fruit of action

anvaya.form: verb, aorist without augment, 2nd person singular (with मा: do not become)

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + कर्मन् (action): not acting

verses.explanation: The most famous sentence in the Gita, and a fourfold precision instrument. One: your adhikāra — jurisdiction, rightful domain — covers the action itself, the only thing actually in your hands. Two: it never covered the fruits, which are settled by a web of causes no agent controls; claiming them is claiming territory you do not own. Three: do not make fruit the *motor* of the act — work driven by reward is work owned by anxiety. Four — the clause that seals Arjuna's last exit — do not therefore slide into loving *inaction*: renouncing work to escape its results is just fruit-fixation wearing robes. What remains is astonishingly clean: full engagement in the deed, full release of the outcome. The archer owns the loosing of the arrow; the wind owns the rest.
verses.connection: Compresses the entire teaching since 2.39 into one rule of life — and shuts the door (clause four) on the very retreat Arjuna proposed in chapter 1.
verses.reflection: Do one task today with full craft and zero claim — your right is to the work alone.
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: What part of your work is actually yours to control?

refs.note: God is the master of all creation, and every moving and unmoving being is his servant, so the fruits of work belong to him.

views.text: Arjuna's right is to action, not yet to steadfastness in knowledge. Craving results makes one the very cause of their production; and one must not slide into inaction thinking 'why do painful work if I want no fruit?'
Acts done without eye on fruit become worship of the Lord and a means to release. Nor should Arjuna see himself as the agent: agency belongs to the guṇas, or to the Lord of all.
A fruit is what one prays for, so it does not befall one who does not desire it; clinging to non-action is itself a tight grip born of false notions and must be dropped.

Thirst for fruits brings repeated births to enjoy them; desireless work purifies the heart, and from purity comes Self-knowledge. Notes karma's range: action, caste-duty, Vedic ritual, and stored tendencies.
The verse gives four rules: do your duty without anxiety over results, know the fruits are for God's pleasure, drop the pride of being the doer, and do not slide into inaction.

verses.devanagari:
योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा धनञ्जय ।
सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
yogasthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā dhanañjaya
siddhyasiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṃ yoga ucyate
verses.essence: Established in yoga, perform actions, abandoning attachment, Dhananjaya — equal in success and failure. Equanimity is called yoga.
verses.translation: Perform action, O Arjuna, being steadfast in Yoga, abandoning attachment and balanced in success and failure. Evenness of mind is called Yoga.

anvaya.parts: योग (yoga) + स्थ (standing in): established in yoga

anvaya.base: धनञ्जय · Dhanañjaya, a name of Arjuna
anvaya.parts: धनम् (wealth) + जय (conquering): winner of wealth
सिद्धि (success) + असिद्धि (failure): success and failure, a paired compound

anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is said)

verses.explanation: And then, the definition — the first of the Gita's great one-line definitions of yoga: samatvaṁ yoga ucyate. Not posture, not breath, not trance: *evenness* is yoga. The verse choreographs the whole stance — stand in the yoked state, *act* (kuru karmāṇi: the command is to do, not to abstain), drop the clinging, stay level through siddhi and asiddhi alike. Evenness is not indifference; the archer still aims with total care. It is the refusal to let the self rise and fall with the arrow's luck. And the definition is given in the middle of an instruction about work, setting yoga's home in the active life. Spoken to 'Dhananjaya', the *winner of wealth*, the name itself becomes the lesson: the great winner is taught the wealth of not needing to win.
verses.connection: States 2.47 positively and crowns it with a definition: what releasing the fruits *produces* in a person is samatva — and that evenness is the whole of yoga.
verses.reflection: Define yoga for yourself this hour: steadiness while acting, evenness while outcomes land.
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: How do you stay steady through both success and failure?

views.text: Act for God alone, yet drop even the attachment 'God will be pleased with me'. Success means the knowledge that dawns from a mind purified by desireless work; failure means its absence.
Concrete: give up attachment to kingdom and kinsmen and fight, level in victory or defeat. The 'yoga' of 'established in yoga' is exactly this evenness about success and failure.
Yoga is exclusive devotion to the Supreme Lord; saṅga is the conceit of being the doer. Evenness is called yoga because it is the collected mind, and even the fruit, knowledge, is left to the Lord.
Knowing that effort is ours and results are God's, we offer the outcome to him and accept whatever comes as his will. Embracing success and failure alike, while still doing our best, is true yoga.

verses.devanagari:
दूरेण ह्यवरं कर्म बुद्धियोगाद्धनञ्जय ।
बुद्धौ शरणमन्विच्छ कृपणाः फलहेतवः॥
verses.transliteration:
dūreṇa hyavaraṃ karma buddhiyogāddhanañjaya
buddhau śaraṇamanviccha kṛpaṇāḥ phalahetavaḥ
verses.essence: Far inferior is mere action to the yoga of understanding, Dhananjaya. Take refuge in understanding — pitiable are those driven by fruits.
verses.translation: Far lower than the Yoga of wisdom is action, O Arjuna. Seek thou refuge in wisdom; wretched are they whose motive is the fruit.

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, instrumental singular used as adverb (by far)

anvaya.parts: बुद्धि (understanding) + योग (discipline): the yoga of understanding

anvaya.base: फलहेतु · one whose motive is the fruit
anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative plural
anvaya.parts: फल (fruit) + हेतु (motive): those whose motive is the fruit

verses.explanation: A ranking, and then a hard word. Action driven by results stands far below action carried by buddhi-yoga — the same deed, transformed by the consciousness performing it. Then kṛpaṇa, the pitiable miser — the word the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad uses for one who leaves this world without knowing the Imperishable. Why miserly? Because the fruit-driven trade the infinite for the finite — they spend a deathless self chasing perishable returns, the worst exchange rate in existence. The remedy is stated as shelter, not technique: buddhau śaraṇam anviccha — take *refuge* in understanding, live from it as from a roof.
verses.connection: Ranks what 2.47–48 distinguished: same outward work, but the inner yoga is the higher thing — and fruit-hunger is spiritual poverty.
verses.reflection: Take refuge in understanding today, not in outcomes — pity the bargainer you were yesterday.
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: Why does working only for rewards leave a person poor at heart?

refs.note: The miserly are those who take the world of sense objects to be the whole of reality.
A miser is one who has no control over the senses.

views.text: Fruit-seeking action is far below action done in the wisdom of equanimity, because it causes birth and death. Take shelter in knowledge of the supreme Goal; the fruit-hungry are pitiable in the sense of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's Gārgī passage.
Śaraṇa means abode: live in that evenness of mind. Action with equanimity ends the sufferings of saṃsāra; action with an eye on results keeps one in it.
Offers a second reading: within this understanding, take refuge in the Lord as one's protector. Buddhi-yoga is karma-yoga done with resolute understanding, or as the means to knowledge.
Work has an outer act and an inner motive. Working for one's own enjoyment is miserly, working for a higher cause is better, and working to offer all fruits to God is true wisdom.

verses.devanagari:
बुद्धियुक्तो जहातीह उभे सुकृतदुष्कृते ।
तस्माद्योगाय युज्यस्व योगः कर्मसु कौशलम्॥
verses.transliteration:
buddhiyukto jahātīha ubhe sukṛtaduṣkṛte
tasmādyogāya yujyasva yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam
verses.essence: One yoked to understanding leaves behind, even here, both good and evil deeds. Therefore yoke yourself to yoga: yoga is skill in action.
verses.translation: Endowed with wisdom (evenness of mind), one casts off in this life both good and evil deeds; therefore, devote thyself to Yoga; Yoga is skill in action.

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular (subject)
anvaya.parts: बुद्धि (understanding) + युक्त (joined, yoked): one joined to understanding

anvaya.base: सुकृत · good deed; दुष्कृत · evil deed
anvaya.parts: सुकृत (good deed) + दुष्कृत (bad deed): virtue and vice, a paired compound

anvaya.form: imperative, 2nd person singular, middle voice (yoke yourself)

verses.explanation: Two thunderclaps in one verse. First: the buddhi-yukta drops *both* sukṛta and duṣkṛta — not evil only, but the whole credit-and-debit ledger of karma. Merit binds as surely as sin (golden chains are chains); freedom is not a high score but the end of scoring, and it happens *iha*, here, not after death. Second, the chapter's second great definition: yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam — yoga is skill in action. The commentaries guard it from misreading: the skill is not technical polish but the art that makes deeds which bind by nature lose their power to bind — acting with everything and being bound by nothing, work so clean it leaves no residue on the worker. Arjuna feared action as a trap; Krishna reveals action, rightly done, as the art form of the free.
verses.connection: Answers Arjuna's terror of sin from 1.36–45 at the root: the yoga of 2.48–49 dissolves the binding power of *all* deeds, white and black alike.
verses.reflection: Bring skill to one action today as worship: yogah karmasu kaushalam — excellence as offering.
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: Does giving up attachment to results make you worse at your work?

views.text: Virtue and vice are shed through purification of mind and the rise of knowledge. Skill is the equanimity, with the mind dedicated to God, that makes actions which bind by their nature give up that nature.
The even-minded doer sheds good and evil karma piled up from beginningless time. 'Skill in action' means that keeping this evenness while acting takes great ability.
Sukṛta leads to heaven, duṣkṛta to hell; both are dropped in this very life by the Lord's grace. The skill is the art of turning binding acts toward liberation by making them worship of Īśvara.
Working without attachment does not reduce skill; it raises it. A surgeon operates calmly on strangers but hands his own child to another, because attachment brings fear that spoils performance.

verses.devanagari:
कर्मजं बुद्धियुक्ता हि फलं त्यक्त्वा मनीषिणः ।
जन्मबन्धविनिर्मुक्ताः पदं गच्छन्त्यनामयम्॥
verses.transliteration:
karmajaṃ buddhiyuktā hi phalaṃ tyaktvā manīṣiṇaḥ
janmabandhavinirmuktāḥ padaṃ gacchantyanāmayam
verses.essence: The wise, yoked to understanding, abandoning the fruit born of action, freed from the bondage of birth, go to the state beyond sorrow.
verses.translation: The wise, possessed of knowledge, having abandoned the fruits of their actions, and being freed from the fetters of birth, go to the place which is beyond all evil.

anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + ज (born): born of action
बुद्धि (understanding) + युक्त (yoked): joined to understanding

anvaya.meaning: freed from the bondage of birth
anvaya.base: जन्मबन्धविनिर्मुक्त · released from the bond of birth
anvaya.parts: जन्म (birth) + बन्ध (bondage) + विनिर्मुक्त (fully freed): fully freed from the bond that is birth
अन् (without) + आमय (disease): free of affliction

verses.explanation: The full trajectory in one sweep: release the fruit → the bond of rebirth unties → arrival at the padam anāmayam, the place without sickness, where nothing aches. The promise answers Arjuna's opening wound with anatomical precision — his grief 'dried up the senses' (2.8), an affliction nothing attainable could cure; here is the unafflicted state, reached not by gaining anything but by *releasing* one thing. The mechanics are exact: what chains a being to the wheel is not action but the hook of expectation inside it. Unhook the fruit, and the wheel has nothing left to grip.
verses.connection: Extends 2.50 to its horizon: the ledger closed in this life becomes freedom from the wheel of birth itself.
verses.reflection: Imagine working a whole week with no thirst for its fruits — taste the freedom in the thought.
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: Where does giving up the fruits of action finally lead the wise?

refs.note: People act for happiness yet never find it; their fruitive works only deepen their misery.

views.text: 'Born of action' goes with 'fruit': the fruit is good or bad bodies. The state is Viṣṇu's supreme state, liberation, and freedom from birth comes even while living; alternatively, buddhi here is enlightenment itself, matured from karma-yoga.
The particle hi signals that this teaching is well known in all the Upaniṣads: the even-minded who give up fruits are freed from rebirth and reach the region beyond all ills.

Everyone pursues happiness through fruitive work and finds misery instead. Those who see God as the true enjoyer offer him all results, accept what comes as his grace, and so escape the bonds of birth and death.

verses.devanagari:
यदा ते मोहकलिलं बुद्धिर्व्यतितरिष्यति ।
तदा गन्तासि निर्वेदं श्रोतव्यस्य श्रुतस्य च॥
verses.transliteration:
yadā te mohakalilaṃ buddhirvyatitariṣyati
tadā gantāsi nirvedaṃ śrotavyasya śrutasya ca
verses.essence: When your understanding crosses beyond the thicket of delusion, then you will reach indifference to what has been heard and what is yet to be heard.
verses.translation: When thy intellect crosses beyond the mire of delusion, then thou shalt attain to indifference as to what has been heard and what has yet to be heard.

anvaya.parts: मोह (delusion) + कलिल (thicket, mire): the tangle that is delusion

anvaya.meaning: of what is yet to be heard
anvaya.form: gerundive (to be heard), neuter, genitive singular (of)

verses.explanation: A milestone is set, with a striking marker. Moha-kalila — delusion as a thicket, a mire, exactly the tangle Arjuna named at 2.7 ('my mind is confused about dharma'). Crossed, it yields nirveda toward śrotavya and śruta — disinterest in all the doctrines yet to be heard and already heard. Scripture-weariness as a sign of *progress*: when the destination is seen, the appetite for more maps quietly dies. The mind stops collecting teachings the way a man who has found water stops collecting descriptions of wells (the flood-image of 2.46 still working underneath).
verses.connection: Begins answering 'how will I know it's working?' — first sign: the compulsive hunger for more answers, more authority, subsides.
verses.reflection: Notice one inherited confusion you have already crossed — the far bank exists; you have touched it.
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: When do you stop caring about everything you have heard and might hear?

refs.note: Having seen that pleasures earned through ritual, here and in heaven, are passing and mixed with misery, the wise turn away from them.

views.text: Delusion is the non-discrimination that confuses Self and not-Self and drives the mind to objects. Once the mind is pure, all that is heard or to be heard apart from Self-knowledge is seen as fruitless.
The tangle is the dense impurity of sin that breeds attachment to petty results; freed of it, Arjuna will of his own accord feel disgust for the results he has heard of and will hear of.

Moha is taking the body for the self, and kalila means a dense thicket, as the lexicon says; the understanding crosses it by the grace of the Lord being worshipped, and stops seeking what it has heard.
An intellect lit by spiritual knowledge sees sense pleasures as sources of misery, so it loses interest in the rituals that promise them.

verses.devanagari:
श्रुतिविप्रतिपन्ना ते यदा स्थास्यति निश्चला ।
समाधावचला बुद्धिस्तदा योगमवाप्स्यसि॥
verses.transliteration:
śrutivipratipannā te yadā sthāsyati niścalā
samādhāvacalā buddhistadā yogamavāpsyasi
verses.essence: When your understanding, bewildered by the scriptures, stands unmoving and steady in samadhi — then you will attain yoga.
verses.translation: When thy intellect, which is perplexed by the Veda text, which thou hast read, shall stand immovable and steady in the Self, then thou shalt attain Self-realisation.

anvaya.parts: श्रुति (scripture, or hearing) + विप्रतिपन्न (perplexed, tossed about): tossed about by what one has heard
निस् (without) + चल (moving): not moving
अ (not) + चल (moving): immovable

verses.explanation: The second milestone, and the destination named. Śruti-vipratipannā — a mind whipsawed by revelation itself, hearing the tradition command war here and ahimsa there (Arjuna's exact predicament). Yoga arrives when that buffeted understanding comes to rest: niścalā, acalā — motionless, unwavering — in samādhi, the gathered depth. Not when the contradictions are resolved on paper, but when the mind no longer needs them resolved to be still. The criterion of arrival is not knowledge but *stillness* — and with that word the teaching pauses, because Arjuna is about to ask his first real question since surrendering: what does such a person actually look like?
verses.connection: Completes the pair begun at 2.52 and lands on 'samadhi' — the word that triggers Arjuna's great question in the next verse.
verses.reflection: Let your mind stand still amid contradictory advice today, unbribed by any of it.
verses.background: Krishna names a second wisdom: buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding in action. Standing in the war-chariot he teaches the right to work without claim on fruits, evenness as yoga, and skill in action — counsel for crossing beyond the bewilderment of all doctrines.
verses.hook: When does a mind confused by many teachings finally become still?

views.text: Śruti means the Vedas with their many ends and means, which toss the mind about. Samādhi is the Self, where the mind is fixed; the yoga attained is enlightenment born of discrimination.

Śruti here means hearing from Krishna, not the Veda, and vipratipannā means specially enlightened. The yoga reached is the vision of the self, which follows from steady wisdom gained through detached work.

The sign of reaching steady understanding is a sense of futility toward scripture heard and to be heard. Arjuna's fear of ruining his race came from impressions left by such teachings and will vanish with them.

Samādhi is the Supreme Lord, 'that in which the mind is placed'; the understanding is niścalā when not pulled by other objects and acalā when made firm by practice, and the yoga gained is knowledge of truth.

Advanced aspirants may wonder if dropping rituals for wholehearted devotion is an offence. The verse answers that staying fixed in devotion, unmoved by ritual rewards, is not wrong but a higher state.

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
स्थितप्रज्ञस्य का भाषा समाधिस्थस्य केशव ।
स्थितधीः किं प्रभाषेत किमासीत व्रजेत किम्॥
verses.transliteration:
sthitaprajñasya kā bhāṣā samādhisthasya keśava
sthitadhīḥ kiṃ prabhāṣeta kimāsīta vrajeta kim
verses.essence: Arjuna asks: What marks the one of steady wisdom, who abides in samadhi, Keshava? How does the steady-minded speak, how sit, how walk?
verses.translation: What, O Krishna, is the description of him who has steady wisdom, and is merged in the superconscious state? How does one of steady wisdom speak, how does he sit, how does he walk?

anvaya.base: स्थितप्रज्ञ · one whose wisdom is steady
anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, genitive singular (of)
anvaya.parts: स्थित (steady, standing) + प्रज्ञा (wisdom): one whose wisdom stands firm
समाधि (absorption) + स्थ (standing in): established in samādhi

anvaya.base: केशव · Keśava, a name of Krishna

anvaya.parts: स्थित (steady) + धी (thought, mind): one whose mind is steady

verses.explanation: Arjuna speaks for the first time since na yotsye (2.9) — and the change in him is the real news. No argument, no lament: a question, and the *right* question. Not 'is this true?' but 'what does it look like when lived?' — kiṁ prabhāṣeta, kim āsīta, vrajeta kim: how does such a one speak, sit, move? He is asking for a portrait, not a proof — the saint described at street level. The tradition treasures this instinct: truth must be visible in a gait, audible in a sentence, or it is only philosophy. The rest of the chapter (2.55–72) is Krishna's answer — the Gita's first full portrait of the liberated human being.
verses.connection: The word 'samadhi' in 2.53 becomes a doorway: the student, fully a student now, asks to *see* the goal in human form.
verses.reflection: Ask of every ideal you admire: how does it walk, sit, speak? Demand the lived version.
verses.background: Arjuna asks his first question of the teaching itself — no longer about the war but about the goal: how does the person of steady wisdom speak, sit, walk? He asks for the portrait of the state being described.
verses.hook: How does a person of steady wisdom speak, sit, and walk?

views.text: Bhāṣā is how others describe the man whose realization 'I am the supreme Brahman' stays steady; the rest asks how he himself speaks, sits and moves.
Treats the verse as several technical questions: is 'sthita-prajña' a name by usage or by etymology, what does 'sthira-dhī' denote, what such a yogin practises, and what he attains.
Bhāṣā means lakṣaṇa, the mark by which someone is known: by what sign is a person called sthita-prajña? His samādhi is natural to him, not effortful.
Arjun wants to know both the inner state of an enlightened person and how it shows in behaviour. This is the first of his sixteen sets of questions that draw out the Gita's teachings.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
प्रजहाति यदा कामान्सर्वान्पार्थ मनोगतान् ।
आत्मन्येवात्मना तुष्टः स्थितप्रज्ञस्तदोच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
prajahāti yadā kāmānsarvānpārtha manogatān
ātmanyevātmanā tuṣṭaḥ sthitaprajñastadocyate
verses.essence: When one fully casts off all desires of the mind, Partha, satisfied in the Self by the Self alone — then one is called steady in wisdom.
verses.translation: When a man completely casts off, O Arjuna, all the desires of the mind and is satisfied in the Self by the Self, then is he said to be one of steady wisdom.

anvaya.parts: मनस् (mind) + गत (gone into): that have entered the mind

anvaya.base: स्थितप्रज्ञ · one whose wisdom is steady
anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular
anvaya.parts: स्थित (steady) + प्रज्ञा (wisdom): one whose wisdom stands firm

anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is said)

verses.explanation: Krishna begins the portrait from the inside — the one mark no onlooker can see, stated first because everything visible follows from it. Prajahāti kāmān sarvān mano-gatān: drops *all* the desires that live in the mind. And the question every hearer asks — what fills the vacancy? — is answered in the same breath: ātmany evātmanā tuṣṭaḥ, content in the Self, *by* the Self — satisfaction that needs no supply line to the world. Every other satisfaction is imported; this one is domestic. Desires are not suppressed by force; they are outgrown by a fullness that arrived from within. The commentators add that these marks of the sage are also the seeker's disciplines: what comes naturally to the one is practised with effort by the other.
verses.connection: The portrait's foundation: before describing how the sage speaks or walks (2.54), name the inner state that makes the walk what it is.
verses.reflection: Find one desire you could release today and discover the self contenting itself by itself.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: What marks a person whose wisdom has become truly steady?

refs.note: When every selfish desire leaves the heart, the mortal becomes free of birth and death and attains Brahman.
Each rank aspires to the next, king to emperor to god to Indra to Brahmā, yet the thirst for enjoyment never ends.

views.text: The marks of the realized are the very disciplines of the aspirant. Contentment in the Self is named so that dropping all desires does not leave one aimless like a madman; the sthita-prajña is a renunciant who delights in the Self.
This is the highest stage of devotion to knowledge: the mind rests on the self within and, content with it, expels every other desire. The following verses describe successively lower stages.
Takes the name etymologically: 'stabilized intellect' means an intellect that has grown permanent roots in the Self, so the agitation of desire from sense-objects ends.
The soul, a fragment of God's bliss, naturally seeks bliss; sought in the world it becomes lust, chasing a mirage. The steady sage renounces such desires and finds contentment within.

verses.devanagari:
दुःखेष्वनुद्विग्नमनाः सुखेषु विगतस्पृहः ।
वीतरागभयक्रोधः स्थितधीर्मुनिरुच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
duḥkheṣvanudvignamanāḥ sukheṣu vigataspṛhaḥ
vītarāgabhayakrodhaḥ sthitadhīrmunirucyate
verses.essence: Unshaken in sorrows, without craving in joys, free of passion, fear and anger — that one is called a sage of steady mind.
verses.translation: He whose mind is not shaken by adversity, who does not hanker after pleasures, and is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady wisdom.

anvaya.base: अनुद्विग्नमनस् · one whose mind is unagitated
anvaya.parts: अनुद्विग्न (unagitated) + मनस् (mind): whose mind is not shaken
विगत (gone away) + स्पृहा (longing): from whom longing has gone

anvaya.meaning: free of attachment, fear and anger
anvaya.base: वीतरागभयक्रोध · rid of passion, fear, anger
anvaya.parts: वीत (gone) + राग (attachment) + भय (fear) + क्रोध (anger): from whom attachment, fear and anger have gone
स्थित (steady) + धी (mind): whose mind is steady

anvaya.form: verb, present passive, 3rd person singular (is said)

verses.explanation: Now the weather test. Sorrows arrive — the mind does not convulse (anudvigna-manāḥ: un-shaken, not un-feeling); joys arrive — no grasping after more of them, no clinging as they pass. Then the triple release that makes this possible: rāga, the pull toward; bhaya, the recoil from what threatens; krodha, the burn when the pull is blocked. These three are one mechanism at different temperatures — and all three are children of dependency on outcomes. Withdraw the dependency (2.55's inner fullness) and the mechanism goes quiet. The sage still stands in the rain and the sun; what is gone is the inner scrambling for shelter.
verses.connection: Tests 2.55's fullness against the two weathers, pain and pleasure — equanimity now shown as lived temperament, not theory.
verses.reflection: In the next small upset, watch for the muni's mark: no spike of craving, fear, or anger.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: How does a wise person stay steady when sorrow or pleasure arrives?

views.text: Muni means the realized monk. Sorrows on the bodily, natural and supernatural planes leave his mind unperturbed, and unlike fire that flares when fed, he does not flare up with longing when delights come.

Defines each term exactly: desire is longing for what is not yet gained, fear is dread of losing the beloved or meeting the unwanted, anger is a disturbance aimed at whoever causes that. This describes a stage just below 2.55.
