Reads the compound as the reason for the first two marks: it is because attachment, fear and anger have left him that sorrow does not shake him and pleasure does not tempt him.
The steady sage is free of craving, fear, and anger. Letting the mind brood over pain or hanker for pleasure pulls it down from divine contemplation, so the sage allows neither.

verses.devanagari:
यः सर्वत्रानभिस्नेहस्तत्तत्प्राप्य शुभाशुभम् ।
नाभिनन्दति न द्वेष्टि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता॥
verses.transliteration:
yaḥ sarvatrānabhisnehastattatprāpya śubhāśubham
nābhinandati na dveṣṭi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā
verses.essence: One without attachment on any side, who meeting good or evil neither rejoices nor recoils — that one's wisdom stands firm.
verses.translation: He who is everywhere without attachment, on meeting with anything good or bad, who neither rejoices not hastes, his wisdom is fixed.

anvaya.parts: अन् (without) + अभिस्नेह (strong attachment, from स्नेह · oil, affection): without sticky attachment
शुभ (good, pleasant) + अशुभ (bad, unpleasant): good and bad taken together

verses.explanation: The refrain that will toll through the rest of the chapter sounds for the first time: tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā — that one's wisdom is *installed*, load-bearing, built on rock. The mark here is subtle: anabhisneha is not coldness but the absence of sneha in its root sense — the *sticky oil* of attachment, the film that makes experiences adhere to the self. Events still arrive, śubha and aśubha, welcome and unwelcome; the sage neither throws a parade nor slams a door. Things pass through such a person the way light passes through clear glass — fully received, nothing retained as residue.
verses.connection: Generalizes 2.56 from great sorrows and joys to the whole stream of daily this-and-that — and coins the chapter's refrain.
verses.reflection: Receive today's good news and bad news with the same face, just once, as an experiment.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: How does a steady person respond when good or bad things happen?

views.text: Anabhisneha means no attachment to anything, even body and life; free of elation and dejection, the renunciant's wisdom born of discrimination stays established.
Describes yet another step down from 2.55–56: indifferent to pleasing objects, feeling no pull or push when meeting or losing them, this person too is of firm wisdom.
Answers Arjuna's 'how does he speak?': he praises nothing pleasant and blames nothing unpleasant, but speaks as one indifferent, without affection even for sons.
Kipling's poem If echoes this description of the steady sage. Its wide appeal shows that the longing for enlightenment is the soul's own nature, found in every culture.

verses.devanagari:
यदा संहरते चायं कूर्मोऽङ्गानीव सर्वशः ।
इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता॥
verses.transliteration:
yadā saṃharate cāyaṃ kūrmo'ṅgānīva sarvaśaḥ
indriyāṇīndriyārthebhyastasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā
verses.essence: And when, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, one withdraws the senses from their objects on every side — that one's wisdom stands firm.
verses.translation: When, like the tortoise which withdraws on all sides its limbs, he withdraws his senses from the sense-objects, then his wisdom becomes steady.

anvaya.parts: इन्द्रिय (sense) + अर्थ (object) — the objects of the senses

verses.explanation: The portrait's first image, and a masterpiece of selection: the tortoise. It draws in its limbs — saṁharate, gathers home — not by cutting them off but by *retracting* them, whole and alive, beneath the shell. So the sage with the five senses: not blinded, not deafened, but capable of recall — attention answers to its owner. The choice of animal does half the teaching: the tortoise does this by nature, without strain, and so the sage's withdrawal is unhurried and effortless, a skill rather than a struggle. And limbs drawn in can be extended again — the senses remain available servants; they have simply ceased to be kidnappers.
verses.connection: From inner state (2.55–57) to the body's gates: the first *practice* visible in the sage — command over where attention goes.
verses.reflection: Practice the tortoise once: feel a provocation, and draw the senses in instead of out.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: How does a tortoise show the way to master the senses?

refs.note: Satisfying desires never ends them; like butter poured on fire, it makes them blaze more strongly.

views.text: 'Fully withdraws' signals absolute firmness and complete control. But a sick man's senses also go quiet while his hankering stays, so outer withdrawal alone is not yet the sage; the next verse shows how the hankering goes.
Withdrawing the senses at the very moment they reach for objects, and fixing the mind on the self, is one of four stages of devotion to knowledge, each perfected by the one after it.
The sage withdraws into his own Self; or, in a second reading, he takes everything from sense-objects to sense-organs back into the Self as his own.
The tortoise is the example of effortless withdrawal: just as it draws in its limbs by its own nature, the yogi pulls the senses back from objects without strain.
Feeding the senses only inflames them, like scratching an itch. The enlightened sage, like a turtle drawing in its limbs, can withdraw or engage the senses at will.

verses.devanagari:
विषया विनिवर्तन्ते निराहारस्य देहिनः ।
रसवर्जं रसोऽप्यस्य परं दृष्ट्वा निवर्तते॥
verses.transliteration:
viṣayā vinivartante nirāhārasya dehinaḥ
rasavarjaṃ raso'pyasya paraṃ dṛṣṭvā nivartate
verses.essence: Sense-objects fall away from the abstinent embodied one — all but the taste. Even the taste departs when the Supreme is seen.
verses.translation: The objects of the senses turn away from the abstinent man leaving the longing (behind); but his longing also turns away on seeing the Supreme.

anvaya.parts: निर् (without) + आहार (taking in, food) — one who takes nothing in
रस (taste, relish) + वर्ज (leaving out) — with the relish excepted

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, accusative singular (object)

verses.explanation: The most psychologically honest verse in the chapter. Abstain, and the *objects* recede — but rasa remains: the taste, the remembered relish, the inner tongue still flavoring what the mouth renounced. Every dieter, every reformed addict, every ascetic knows this residue; willpower can starve the behavior but not the savor, and a craving merely caged is a craving waiting. The cure is not more force but a *better taste*: paraṁ dṛṣṭvā — when the Supreme is actually seen, tasted, the lesser rasa falls away on its own, the way a child's sweets lose their kingdom the day something finer is known. Renunciation, the Gita insists, is completed not by subtraction but by encounter.
verses.connection: The honest footnote to 2.58: retraction controls exposure, not appetite — only the sight of the Higher dissolves the root-relish.
verses.reflection: Be patient with cravings that fade but still whisper — only a higher taste retires them fully.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: Why does craving linger even after you stop indulging the senses?

refs.note: God is bliss itself; on attaining him the soul becomes fully content.

views.text: Rasa is the subtle attachment that abstinence cannot touch; it falls away only on realising Brahman as 'I am That'. Discrimination removes gross attachment first, and the knowledge that follows removes the subtle seeds, so there is no vicious circle.
The supreme seen here is the self: hankering goes once one sees that the self is higher than sense-objects and that its experience gives greater joy than they do.
The ascetic who avoids objects still keeps a longing in his inner organ, so he is not yet steady; the man of Yoga has no such longing because he has seen the Supreme Lord.
Nirāhāra can also mean the fasting man: hunger dulls interest in sound and touch, but the craving for taste stays. That craving dies on its own once the Supreme Self is seen.

Fasting or forced restraint only weakens desire for a while, because the soul's thirst for divine bliss remains. When devotion gives that higher taste, lower cravings fall away for good; the Gita teaches sublimation, not suppression.

verses.devanagari:
यततो ह्यपि कौन्तेय पुरुषस्य विपश्चितः ।
इन्द्रियाणि प्रमाथीनि हरन्ति प्रसभं मनः॥
verses.transliteration:
yatato hyapi kaunteya puruṣasya vipaścitaḥ
indriyāṇi pramāthīni haranti prasabhaṃ manaḥ
verses.essence: For even of the striving, discerning man, Kaunteya, the turbulent senses carry off the mind by force.
verses.translation: The turbulent senses, O Arjuna, do violently carry away the mind of a wise man though he be striving (to control them).

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, genitive singular (of one striving)
adjective, neuter, nominative plural (describing the senses)

verses.explanation: Lest the portrait breed complacency, a storm warning. Even the yatat, the one actively striving, even the vipaścit, the discerning — the senses remain pramāthīni, churning, riot-prone, and they haranti, *carry off*, the mind prasabham, *by force*: the language of abduction. No achievement retires the risk; vigilance is not a phase of the path but its permanent climate. There is deep kindness folded into the severity: if the senses can storm even the wise, then Arjuna's own past defeats are not proof of worthlessness — they are the standard weather of embodiment, to be answered with watchfulness rather than shame.
verses.connection: Counterweight to 2.58–59: the tortoise's skill is real but never automatic — the chapter refuses to let mastery sound easy.
verses.reflection: Respect the senses' strength today; the wise are wary precisely because they know the pull.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: Can the senses overpower even a wise person who is trying hard?

refs.note: After thousands of years of indulgence, Saubhari laments his fall and warns others not to seek happiness through material acquisition.

views.text: 'Even' can go with the striving or with the wise man: the senses first confound one drawn to objects, then sweep away a mind that has discrimination, even while he knows what is happening.
Sense control depends on seeing the self, and seeing the self depends on sense control; this mutual dependence is why firm wisdom is so hard to reach.
The senses are like horses: kept under control they carry you to the goal, but turbulent ones throw you down into sense-objects on the way.
The senses are like wild horses newly harnessed. The story of Saubhari, a great sage drawn from meditation into endless indulgence, shows how they can derail even advanced yogis.

verses.devanagari:
तानि सर्वाणि संयम्य युक्त आसीत मत्परः ।
वशे हि यस्येन्द्रियाणि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता॥
verses.transliteration:
tāni sarvāṇi saṃyamya yukta āsīta matparaḥ
vaśe hi yasyendriyāṇi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā
verses.essence: Restraining them all, one should sit yoked, intent on Me. For whose senses are mastered, that one's wisdom stands firm.
verses.translation: Having restrained them all he should sit steadfast, intent on Me; his wisdom is steady whose senses are under control.

anvaya.parts: मद् (me) + पर (highest) — one for whom I am the highest

verses.explanation: Into a discourse that has been austerely impersonal — self, gunas, buddhi — falls one small bomb of a word: mat-paraḥ, *intent on Me*. For the first time the teaching names Krishna himself as the one to hold supreme. The logic is practical before it is theological: the mind cannot hold a vacuum; senses restrained from objects must be given somewhere *better* to rest, and an abstraction makes a poor resting place. A person — the divine charioteer two feet away — can be loved, and love concentrates as discipline alone never will. Here, in a single compound, the entire bhakti of chapters 7–12 sends its first green shoot above the soil.
verses.connection: Supplies what 2.60's warning demands: restraint alone is unstable — the senses need not a cage but a Center, and Krishna quietly offers himself.
verses.reflection: Anchor the senses in something higher before the storm, not during it — sit for two minutes now.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: Once the senses are restrained, where should the mind be placed?

refs.note: King Ambarīṣa engaged every sense, mind, speech, eyes, ears, hands and feet, in the service of Krishna, and so subdued them all.

views.text: Mat-paraḥ means taking Vāsudeva, the inmost Self of all, as the supreme: one sits thinking 'I am not different from Him', and the senses come under control by that practice.
Fixing the mind on the Lord breaks the deadlock between sense control and self-vision: He burns away the mind's impurities, and only then can it master the senses. Self-effort alone fails.
The senses are restrained by the mind, not by mere inactivity, with attention resting on nothing but the Supreme Lord, the Consciousness-Self.
Restraint alone is not enough; the tamed senses need a proper engagement, which is absorption in devotion to God, as King Ambarish showed by using every sense in God's service.

verses.devanagari:
ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते ।
सङ्गात्सञ्जायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते॥
verses.transliteration:
dhyāyato viṣayānpuṃsaḥ saṅgasteṣūpajāyate
saṅgātsañjāyate kāmaḥ kāmātkrodho'bhijāyate
verses.essence: Brooding on sense-objects, attachment to them is born; from attachment springs desire; from desire, anger is born.
verses.translation: When a man thinks of the objects, attachment for them arises; from attachment desire is born; from desire anger arises.

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, genitive singular (of one thinking)

verses.explanation: Now the autopsy of a fall — the Gita's famous causal chain, and its first link is the masterstroke: not contact with objects but dhyāyataḥ, *brooding* on them, attention parked on an object. Ruin begins as meditation pointed the wrong way; the mind circling an object is already worshiping it. Repetition warms thought into saṅga, attachment (the stickiness of 2.57 returning); saṅga ripens into kāma, desire; and desire, the moment the world blocks it, ignites as krodha. Anger is desire thwarted. Note what this chain quietly absolves: the object itself. The mango is innocent; the *rehearsal* of the mango is where the avalanche starts. The defense, therefore, begins with attention: guard where the mind parks.
verses.connection: Explains the abduction of 2.60 frame by frame: how the senses' coup actually unfolds — beginning not at the gates but in the throne room of attention.
verses.reflection: Catch one thought today at the brooding stage — before it becomes desire, then anger, then ruin.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: How does merely thinking about something lead to anger?

refs.note: Even all the world's wealth and pleasures cannot satisfy one gripped by desire, so the wise give desire up.
Lust, anger and greed are diseases of the mind that nearly everyone suffers yet few recognize; and satisfying desire only feeds greed.

views.text: What one dwells on is the charm imagined in objects; attachment hardens into thirst, and when anything obstructs that thirst, anger springs up.

For one who controls the senses but has not fixed the mind on the Lord, brooding on objects is unavoidable because of impressions from beginningless time; anger then turns on whoever seems to block the desire.
Having shown the danger of uncontrolled outer senses, the verse turns to the uncontrolled mind: it broods on objects as if they were good, and the chain begins.
Repeatedly imagining happiness in an object breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, fulfilled desire breeds greed, and blocked desire breeds anger. These are diseases of the mind.

verses.devanagari:
क्रोधाद्भवति सम्मोहः सम्मोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः ।
स्मृतिभ्रंशाद् बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति॥
verses.transliteration:
krodhādbhavati sammohaḥ sammohātsmṛtivibhramaḥ
smṛtibhraṃśād buddhināśo buddhināśātpraṇaśyati
verses.essence: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, loss of memory; from lost memory, the ruin of understanding — and when understanding is ruined, one is lost.
verses.translation: From anger comes delusion; from delusion loss of memory; from loss of memory the destruction of discrimination; from the destruction of discrimination he perishes.

anvaya.parts: स्मृति (memory) + विभ्रम (straying, confusion) — memory gone astray
स्मृति (memory) + भ्रंश (falling away) — the collapse of memory
बुद्धि (understanding) + नाश (destruction) — the destruction of understanding
बुद्धि (understanding) + नाश (destruction)

verses.explanation: The chain's second half, where psychology becomes free fall. Anger thickens into sammoha — the fog in which right and wrong can no longer be told apart; the fog scatters smṛti — not data-memory but *remembrance* of what one has learned and resolved (every furious person forgets themselves first). With remembrance gone, buddhi — the faculty this whole chapter has labored to build — collapses; and with buddhi gone, praṇaśyati: the person is ruined, no arrow required. Eight links from a daydream to a ruin. The chain's mercy is its precision: a sequence this exact can be cut, and the scissors work best at link one. Note the echo near the poem's end: Arjuna's smṛtir labdhā, 'memory regained' (18.73), is this forgetting undone.
verses.connection: Completes 2.62's avalanche to the bottom — Arjuna's own chapter-one collapse, traced in slow motion, now legible as a sequence rather than a fate.
verses.reflection: Memorize the chain: anger, delusion, broken memory, lost discernment — and guard the first link.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: What happens to your judgment once anger takes hold?

views.text: The memory lost is the memory of what scripture and teacher taught, so an angry man may abuse even his teacher. A person is himself only while he can tell right from wrong; losing that, he is unfit for life's goal.
What is forgotten is one's earlier effort at sense control, so its fruit is undone; 'perishing' means sinking back into saṃsāra.
The ascetic gives up objects by thinking of them, and that very thinking starts the chain; giving up objects is harmless only for one whose wisdom is already steady.
Loss of buddhi means consciousness overpowered, as in trees, and 'he perishes' means he becomes like one dead.
Anger clouds the intellect like mist over sunlight, so memory of right and wrong is confused, the intellect is destroyed, and since it is our inner guide, one is ruined.

verses.devanagari:
रागद्वेषवियुक्तैस्तु विषयानिन्द्रियैश्चरन् ।
आत्मवश्यैर्विधेयात्मा प्रसादमधिगच्छति॥
verses.transliteration:
rāgadveṣaviyuktaistu viṣayānindriyaiścaran
ātmavaśyairvidheyātmā prasādamadhigacchati
verses.essence: But the self-governed one, moving among objects with senses freed from craving and aversion, held in the Self's command — attains serenity.
verses.translation: But the self-controlled man, moving among the objects with the senses under restraint and free from attraction and repulsion, attains to peace.

anvaya.base: रागद्वेषवियुक्त · free of attraction and aversion
anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, instrumental plural (with, describing the senses)
anvaya.parts: राग (attraction) + द्वेष (aversion) + वियुक्त (separated) — separated from attraction and aversion

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, nominative singular (while moving)

anvaya.parts: आत्मन् (self) + वश्य (obedient) — obedient to the self

anvaya.base: विधेयात्मन् · one whose mind is obedient
anvaya.parts: विधेय (obedient, governable) + आत्मन् (self, mind) — one whose mind can be governed

verses.explanation: The counter-picture, and a crucial correction of scope: caran viṣayān — *moving among objects*. The free person is not the one who fled the marketplace but the one who walks through it with senses ātma-vaśya, answering to their owner, scrubbed of the twin magnets rāga and dveṣa. Same shops, same colors, same noise; nothing in the scene has hooks anymore. The prize is named prasāda — a beautiful double word: serenity, and the *grace-offering* returned from a shrine. Tranquility, the verse hints, is what the world hands back to the one who stopped grabbing at it.
verses.connection: Answers 2.62–63 point for point: the same senses, the same objects — but with the magnets removed, the avalanche has nothing to start from.
verses.reflection: Move through the same world today minus the clinging, and notice serenity arriving uninvited.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.text_note: Variant: rāga-dveṣa-vimuktaiḥ for -viyuktaiḥ; Śaṅkara, Gita Supersite and the critical edition read viyuktaiḥ (used here).
verses.hook: How can you live among sense objects and still find peace?

views.text: Objects cannot be avoided, so the seeker meets them through senses that are free of attraction and aversion and under his control; here 'ātman' means the mind that can be subdued at will.
With the mind fixed on the Lord and its impurities burnt away, he goes among objects while holding them cheap; his serenity is a mind freed of impurity.
Even while enjoying objects with tamed senses he reaches peace; this answers Arjuna's fourth question, how the steady one moves about.

Since the soul cannot stop seeking happiness, the answer is to seek it in God. Attachment to God purifies the mind; free of material liking and dislike, one receives grace and uses objects without being drawn by them.

verses.devanagari:
प्रसादे सर्वदुःखानां हानिरस्योपजायते ।
प्रसन्नचेतसो ह्याशु बुद्धिः पर्यवतिष्ठते॥
verses.transliteration:
prasāde sarvaduḥkhānāṃ hānirasyopajāyate
prasannacetaso hyāśu buddhiḥ paryavatiṣṭhate
verses.essence: In serenity is born the end of all sorrows; for the clear-hearted, the understanding quickly stands firm.
verses.translation: In that peace all pains are destroyed; for the intellect of the tranquil-minded soon becomes steady.

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, locative singular (in/when there is)

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + दुःख (sorrow) — all sorrows

anvaya.base: प्रसन्नचेतस् · one whose mind is clear
anvaya.parts: प्रसन्न (clear, calm) + चेतस् (mind) — one whose mind is calm

anvaya.base: परि + अव + √स्था · to stand firm all round

verses.explanation: What serenity is *for*. In prasāda, sorrows lose their purchase — sarva-duḥkhānāṁ hāniḥ, the waning of all of them — because suffering's real habitat was never events but the turbid mind that received them. And then a word of tempo, rare in this patient chapter: āśu, *swiftly*. In a clear heart, wisdom settles fast — the way sediment needs only stillness, not effort, to sink. All the chapter's labor (restraint, refuge, evenness) turns out to be the making of stillness; once the water is calm, clarity is not achieved but simply *happens*.
verses.connection: Pays out 2.64's prasāda: serenity is not the path's decoration but its engine — the condition in which the steady buddhi finally takes hold by itself.
verses.reflection: When the heart clears even briefly, watch how quickly the intellect steadies — peace works fast.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: What happens to sorrow once the mind becomes truly serene?

views.text: The serene mind's wisdom becomes steady on every side, like the sky, unmoving as the Self. So the seeker should meet only necessary, scripturally allowed objects, with senses free of love and hate.
The sorrows that end are those born of contact with matter; once the mind is free of what blocks self-vision, the buddhi at once settles on the pure self.

By grace God grants divine knowledge, love, and bliss. Tasting that bliss ends the hankering for sense pleasure, and the intellect, now convinced by experience rather than scripture alone, rests firmly in God.

verses.devanagari:
नास्ति बुद्धिरयुक्तस्य न चायुक्तस्य भावना ।
न चाभावयतः शान्तिरशान्तस्य कुतः सुखम्॥
verses.transliteration:
nāsti buddhirayuktasya na cāyuktasya bhāvanā
na cābhāvayataḥ śāntiraśāntasya kutaḥ sukham
verses.essence: For the unyoked there is no understanding, nor contemplation; without contemplation, no peace — and without peace, where is happiness?
verses.translation: There is no knowledge of the Self to the unsteady and to the unsteady no meditation is possible, and to the unmeditative there can be no peace, and to the man who has no peace, how can there be happiness?

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + युक्त (yoked) — one who is not yoked
अ (not) + युक्त (yoked)

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, genitive singular (for one not doing)
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + भावयत् (contemplating) — one who does not contemplate
अ (not) + शान्त (peaceful)

verses.explanation: The same staircase, descended. The ayukta — unyoked, the mind scattered across its branches (2.41 returning) — has no steady buddhi; without it, no bhāvanā, the dwelling-power of sustained attention; without dwelling, no śānti; and then the question that ends every hedonist's argument before it starts: aśāntasya kutaḥ sukham — for the peaceless, *where* would happiness even live? The unanswerable rhetorical question is the point: pleasure poured into a churning mind is water poured into a cracked pot. Arjuna sought a formula for happiness in chapter one — kingdom? family? — and here is the audit: every route runs through peace, and peace runs through the yoked mind. There is no detour.
verses.connection: The negative image of 2.64–65: the four-step ladder shown from below, proving there is no path to sukha that bypasses the gathered buddhi.
verses.reflection: No peace without focus, no happiness without peace — trace today's restlessness back up this chain.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: Can someone without inner discipline ever find real peace and happiness?

views.text: Bhāvanā is an earnest longing for Self-knowledge, and śānti is restraint of the senses. Real happiness is the senses' freedom from thirst; while thirst lasts there is not an iota of it.
One who controls the senses by his own effort, without fixing his mind on the Lord, never gains the understanding of the pure self; will power alone ends in failure.
Bhāvanā is meditation, which is what settles the buddhi in the self; the happiness that never comes to the restless is the bliss of liberation.
Without disciplining mind and senses one cannot meditate on God or taste his bliss, and without that higher taste one stays trapped in sense pleasures, like the bee that dies inside a lotus.

verses.devanagari:
इन्द्रियाणां हि चरतां यन्मनोऽनुविधीयते ।
तदस्य हरति प्रज्ञां वायुर्नावमिवाम्भसि॥
verses.transliteration:
indriyāṇāṃ hi caratāṃ yanmano'nuvidhīyate
tadasya harati prajñāṃ vāyurnāvamivāmbhasi
verses.essence: For the mind that follows the roving senses carries off wisdom, as wind carries a ship on the waters.
verses.translation: For the mind, which follows in the wake of the wandering senses, carries away his discrimination, as the wind (carries away) a boat on the waters.

anvaya.form: present participle, neuter, genitive plural (of those moving)

anvaya.base: अनु + वि + √धा · to follow, conform to
anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is made to follow)

verses.explanation: The chapter's nautical image, perfectly engineered. A ship has rudder, cargo, destination; the wind has none — only force and whim. Let the mind anuvidhīyate, *follow along after* the roving senses, and the whole vessel of wisdom is dragged off course; and one open sail is enough — read closely, even the single sense the mind trails after suffices for the hijack. The image dignifies even as it warns: you are not driftwood, you are a *ship* — built for crossing, equipped to steer. Wreckage is not fate; it is helmsmanship declined.
verses.connection: Compresses the chains of 2.62–63 and the ladder of 2.66 into one picture: the mind's allegiance — rudder or wind — decides everything.
verses.reflection: Mind one wandering sense today like a helmsman minds wind — one gust can take the whole ship.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: How can a single wandering sense carry your wisdom away?

refs.note: The Creator made the senses face outward, so they naturally run toward external objects.

views.text: As wind drives a boat off its intended course, the mind busy with objects turns wisdom, born of discriminating Self from not-Self, away from the Self and towards objects.
A mind allowed to trail the senses loses its leaning towards the pure self and tilts towards objects, carried off as a contrary wind takes a ship.
Even one untamed sense that the mind follows is enough to scatter wisdom, let alone many; it is like wind spinning the boat of a careless helmsman on the sea.
The senses are made to look outward. Deer, bee, fish, moth, and elephant each die through one sense; a person indulging all five is in far greater danger.

verses.devanagari:
तस्माद्यस्य महाबाहो निगृहीतानि सर्वशः ।
इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता॥
verses.transliteration:
tasmādyasya mahābāho nigṛhītāni sarvaśaḥ
indriyāṇīndriyārthebhyastasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā
verses.essence: Therefore, mighty-armed one, whose senses are wholly withheld from their objects — that one's wisdom stands firm.
verses.translation: Therefore, O mighty-armed Arjuna, his knowledge is steady whose senses are completely restrained from sense-objects.

anvaya.parts: महा (great) + बाहु (arm) — one whose arms are mighty
इन्द्रिय (sense) + अर्थ (object) — the objects of the senses

verses.explanation: The tasmāt — *therefore* — that gathers the whole excursion (2.60–67) and closes the ring: the verse all but repeats 2.58, and the refrain prajñā pratiṣṭhitā tolls for the last time. But the same words return heavier. At 2.58 the tortoise was an introduction; now it arrives proven — through the storm warning, the anatomy of the fall, the counter-picture, the ship. Mahābāho, mighty-armed: Krishna salutes the warrior's strength while relocating it — the arms that drew Gandiva are now invited to a harder pull, the inward one. What is repeated after the proof is no longer a description but a verdict.
verses.connection: Closes the loop opened at 2.58: the tortoise-teaching restated as a verdict, now carrying the full weight of everything between.
verses.reflection: Withdraw deliberately from one stimulation today, and notice wisdom getting room to stand.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: Whose wisdom finally becomes firm and settled?

views.text: 'Completely' means the organs in all their kinds, the mind included, held back from objects such as sound.
Summing up 2.64–68: one who controls the mind is not tossed by waves of anger and the rest even while enjoying objects, and so he alone is the man of Yoga.
The address 'mighty-armed' hints that Arjuna, able to subdue enemies, is able to subdue these as well.

In the enlightened, knowledge rules the intellect, the intellect rules the mind, and the mind reins in the senses. In the conditioned state this order is reversed and the senses drag the intellect off course.

verses.devanagari:
या निशा सर्वभूतानां तस्यां जागर्ति संयमी ।
यस्यां जाग्रति भूतानि सा निशा पश्यतो मुनेः॥
verses.transliteration:
yā niśā sarvabhūtānāṃ tasyāṃ jāgarti saṃyamī
yasyāṃ jāgrati bhūtāni sā niśā paśyato muneḥ
verses.essence: What is night for all beings, there the restrained one is awake; where beings wake, that is night for the seeing sage.
verses.translation: That which is night to all beings, in that the self-controlled man is awake; when all beings are awake, that is night for the Muni (sage) who sees.

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + भूत (being) — all beings

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, genitive singular (of one seeing)

verses.explanation: The most haunting verse of the chapter — a chiasmus of two inverted days. The reality in which the sage is wide awake (the Self, the changeless) is pitch night to the world: invisible, unsuspected, slept through. The reality in which the world conducts its blazing noon — profit, rank, fear, prize — is night to the muni: he is not drawn into it; its shapes hold no pull for him. Neither party is simply *blind*; each is asleep precisely where the other lives. It is the gentlest statement of an immense claim: the sage and the world are not on one spectrum of more and less wisdom — they are facing opposite ways. To begin this path is to accept a reversed clock, and a certain solitude of schedule.
verses.connection: After the practice (2.58–68), the strangeness: a quiet warning and a deep comfort — the steadied one will be a foreigner in the world's daylight.
verses.reflection: What the world calls necessary may be your night; where you wake may look like sleep to them.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: How does a sage see the world differently from everyone else?

views.text: The supreme Reality is night to the unenlightened, as day is night to owls. The world of subject and object is night to the sage, which is why rites and duties apply only in ignorance, not after knowledge.
The night is the understanding whose object is the self, obscure to everyone; the restrained one is awake there, while the sense-objects others are busy with lie in darkness for him.
The night is delusive Māyā: the sage stays awake in it, watching how to root it out, and is 'asleep' to worldly business, paying no heed to the pleasure Māyā seems to offer.
Day and night are figurative here, not a call to give up sleep. Worldly people see sense enjoyment as day and its lack as night; the wise see it the other way round.

verses.devanagari:
आपूर्यमाणमचलप्रतिष्ठं
समुद्रमापः प्रविशन्ति यद्वत् ।
तद्वत्कामा यं प्रविशन्ति सर्वे
स शान्तिमाप्नोति न कामकामी॥
verses.transliteration:
āpūryamāṇamacalapratiṣṭhaṃ samudramāpaḥ praviśanti yadvat
tadvatkāmā yaṃ praviśanti sarve sa śāntimāpnoti na kāmakāmī
verses.essence: As waters enter the ocean — ever filled, unmoving in its bed — so all desires enter such a one, who attains peace; not the desirer of desires.
verses.translation: He attains peace into whom all desires enter as waters enter the ocean which, filled from all sides, remains unmoved; but not the man who is full of desires.

anvaya.form: present participle, passive, masculine, accusative singular (being filled)
adjective, masculine, accusative singular (describing the ocean)
anvaya.parts: अचल (unmoving) + प्रतिष्ठा (foundation) — whose foundation does not move
काम (object of desire) + कामिन् (one who desires) — one who keeps wanting desirable things

verses.explanation: The chapter's crowning image. Rivers pour into the ocean continuously, yet it does not flood: āpūryamāṇam, being filled, and acala-pratiṣṭham, its level unmoved. So with the sage: objects and desires still *enter* — praviśanti, the verse is frank, the sage is no sealed vault — but they enter a vastness already complete and vanish without raising the waterline. Against this stands the kāma-kāmī, the desirer of desires, a creek in drought begging every cloud. The difference is not what flows in; it is the depth of what receives. Peace, on this image, is not the absence of input but fullness so established that nothing arriving can add to it — and nothing withheld can wound it.
verses.connection: Resolves the chapter's central question — how to live amid stimulation (2.64) — with its definitive image: not the dam, but the sea.
verses.reflection: Be the ocean once today: let something flow into you without raising your level.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: Who stays at peace while desires keep flowing in like rivers?

views.text: Desires enter him from every side yet vanish in the Self without bringing it under their sway; the peace he attains is liberation, which the one who craves objects never reaches.
Sense-objects reach him and leave only impressions, no reaction; content with the vision of the self, he is undisturbed whether they come or not, as the sea neither rises nor falls.
Objects still come to the sage, pushed by his prārabdha karma, but he stays unchanged inside, like the sea that keeps its bounds however many rivers fill it.
Like the ocean that neither overflows nor shrinks however many rivers pour in, the realized sage stays unmoved whether sense objects are present or absent, and only such a person finds true peace.

verses.devanagari:
विहाय कामान्यः सर्वान्पुमांश्चरति निःस्पृहः ।
निर्ममो निरहङ्कारः स शान्तिमधिगच्छति॥
verses.transliteration:
vihāya kāmānyaḥ sarvānpumāṃścarati niḥspṛhaḥ
nirmamo nirahaṅkāraḥ sa śāntimadhigacchati
verses.essence: The one who abandons all desires and moves free of longing, without 'mine', without 'I' — that one attains peace.
verses.translation: That man attains peace who, abandoning all desires, moves about without longing, without the sense of mine and without egoism.

anvaya.parts: निर् (without) + स्पृहा (longing) — one without longing
निर् (without) + मम (mine) — one with no sense of 'mine'
निर् (without) + अहङ्कार (the 'I'-maker, ego) — one free of ego

verses.explanation: The ocean-image translated into a way of walking: carati, he *moves about* — in the world, on its roads — stripped of three things, each subtler than the last. Niḥspṛhaḥ, no reaching; nirmamaḥ, no 'mine' — and the Gita's very first verse turned on māmakāḥ, *my* people (1.1): the war itself began in that pronoun; finally nirahaṅkāraḥ, no 'I'-maker — the root from which every 'mine' ever grew. The sequence is an excavation: behavior, then possession, then the possessor. What remains when even the claimant is surrendered? Not a void — the verse answers with its verb: peace, śānti, walking around on two feet.
verses.connection: Brings 2.70's ocean ashore: the same fullness as a human gait — and quietly closes the wound of 1.1 by dissolving its pronoun.
verses.reflection: Drop the words 'I' and 'mine' for one hour and watch how many burdens were grammatical.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: What must you give up to live at peace?

views.text: He wanders making effort only to keep the body alive, without longing even for that and without claiming as 'mine' what he needs; free of pride in learning, he attains the peace called nirvāṇa, oneness with Brahman.
The sense of 'mine' towards objects comes from mistaking the body, which is not the self, for the self; one who drops it attains peace by seeing the self.
Because he is free of ego, he has no 'mine' towards the means of enjoyment; inwardly turned, he takes whatever prārabdha brings, wherever he goes, and finds peace.
Peace is disturbed by material desire, greed, ego, and the sense of ownership. Since everything belongs to God and we leave empty-handed, letting these go is the path to inner peace.

verses.devanagari:
एषा ब्राह्मी स्थितिः पार्थ नैनां प्राप्य विमुह्यति ।
स्थित्वास्यामन्तकालेऽपि ब्रह्मनिर्वाणमृच्छति॥
verses.transliteration:
eṣā brāhmī sthitiḥ pārtha naināṃ prāpya vimuhyati
sthitvāsyāmantakāle'pi brahmanirvāṇamṛcchati
verses.essence: This is the state of Brahman, Partha. Attaining it, one is deluded no more. Established in it even at the hour of death, one reaches the nirvana of Brahman.
verses.translation: This is the Brahmic seat (eternal state), O son of Pritha. Attaining to this, none is deluded. Being established therein, even at the end of life, one attains to oneness with Brahman.

anvaya.meaning: at the time of the end
anvaya.parts: अन्त (end) + काल (time) — the time of the end
ब्रह्मन् (Brahman) + निर्वाण (blowing out, final peace) — the final peace that is Brahman

verses.explanation: The chapter sets its seal. Everything since 2.55 — the contentment, the tortoise, the ocean — is now given its true name: brāhmī sthitiḥ, the standing-in-Brahman, a *state*, not an experience that visits and departs. Its first property answers the chapter's first diagnosis: na vimuhyati — no relapse into the delusion that felled Arjuna. Its last answers his deepest dread: held antakāle 'pi, even at the hour of death, it opens into brahma-nirvāṇa — the blowing-out not of the self but of every flame that burned. The teaching that began with a man collapsed between two armies ends with a state no collapse can revoke. What remains, sixteen chapters of it, is Arjuna learning to ask: but how do I *live* this?
verses.connection: Names and seals the whole portrait (2.55–71) — and answers chapter one's wounds: delusion, paralysis, and grief before death.
verses.reflection: Hold the brahmi sthiti as your evening thought: a state one can reach even at the last hour.
verses.background: Krishna answers with the sthita-prajna portrait, the close of the chapter the tradition calls the Gita in miniature: desires released, the tortoise-withdrawal of senses, the chain from brooding to ruin, the ocean-like peace — ending with the Brahman-state that holds even at the hour of death.
verses.hook: What becomes of someone who reaches this state, even at life's end?

refs.note: The wise forever behold the supreme abode of Viṣṇu; once the soul attains God, illusion never overpowers it again.

views.text: The state is living on as one with Brahman after renouncing all action. If even one who reaches it in life's last years is liberated, how much more one who stays in Brahman from youth.
The brāhmī state is disinterested work grounded in knowing the eternal self; the 'brahman' reached is the self, made of bliss, and the chapter's whole teaching aims at this firm wisdom.
One whose heart is purified by worshipping the Lord reaches this state; even a single moment in it at death brings dissolution in Brahman, let alone a lifetime.
Following Vidyāraṇya, 'the end' can mean the moment ignorance, the mutual superimposition of Self and not-Self, comes to an end.
When the heart is purified, God's grace grants God-realization: past karmas, ignorance, and the hold of material nature end. The soul is liberated while living and reaches God's abode at death.
